docs.title: Straight Talk #1: “Data centers are why my power bill went up.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #1 · What people say

# “Data centers are why my power bill went up.”

Our verdict
Overstated, with a real local risk.

Studies of 2015 to 2025 find small effects on home bills, sometimes lower prices. The risk is real where power is already tight.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] A causal study led by EPRI found that where data center capacity doubled, residential electricity prices fell about 4%, over 2015 to 2024.
Source: EPRI, “Have Data Centers Raised Your Electric Bill?” (Watten, Bistline, and Blanford, 2026)

-
[VERIFIED] A Wharton and Harvard Business School working paper estimates that data centers built from 2020 to 2025 explain about 4% of the rise in home electricity prices over that period, and about 15% of the rise in industrial prices. The paper had not been peer reviewed when it was reported.
Source: Rana, Kaps, and Netessine, “The Cost of Intelligence” (Sept. 30, 2026), as summarized by FourWeekMBA from the paper's abstract

-
[VERIFIED] Where the grid was already congested, the story differs. A study for the Edison Electric Institute found PJM, the grid operator for much of the Mid-Atlantic, to be the one area where data centers have raised rates.
Source: E&E News, Plautz and Marshall (Mar. 19, 2026)

-
[PLAUSIBLE] Whether your bill rises depends on your utility's terms. A big new customer that doesn't pay for its own substation or sign a long contract shifts risk onto everyone else on the system.

Where the critics are right
In PJM, where the grid was already congested, rates have gone up because of data centers (E&E News, above). And without a large-load tariff, members can end up paying for a substation built for one customer. [PLAUSIBLE] That worry is fair.

## What to ask for, in writing

- A large-load tariff: a separate rate class for big new customers.

- A minimum bill, so they pay for the capacity they reserve.

- A long contract and an exit fee, so members don't inherit the substation if they leave.

- Collateral, and upgrades paid for up front.

docs.title: Straight Talk #2: “A data center will drain our water.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #2 · What people say

# “A data center will drain our water.”

Our verdict
It depends on the cooling.

A large data center can use millions of gallons a day; one closed-loop design plans for about what 65 homes use. Ask which kind before you argue.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] Large data centers can use up to 5 million gallons of water a day, about what a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people uses. Cooling by evaporation is the water-hungry kind.
Source: Environmental and Energy Study Institute, Yañez-Barnuevo (June 25, 2025)

-
[VERIFIED] A closed-loop campus planned in Port Washington, Wisconsin, expects peak daily use of less than 22,000 gallons, which the developer compared to about 65 homes. Its closed-loop cooling would draw on the city water supply only in emergencies.
Source: TMJ4 News (Sept. 19, 2025), quoting Vantage Data Centers and the city's mayor

-
[VERIFIED] About three-quarters of the U.S. data center water footprint is indirect, at the power plants that supply the electricity, not at the building.
Source: Siddik, Shehabi, and Marston (2021), Environmental Research Letters

-
[PLAUSIBLE] So a closed-loop design moves some of the water question to the power plant: dry cooling saves water on site by using more electricity, and electricity takes water upstream.

Where the critics are right
A design that cools by evaporation really can strain a local water supply, especially in a drought. [PLAUSIBLE] Asking hard questions here is reasonable.

## What to ask for, in writing

- The cooling type, in writing.

- Peak and average daily gallons, and where the water comes from.

- A drought clause that cuts use during water emergencies.

docs.title: Straight Talk #3: “It'll bring hundreds of jobs.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #3 · What people say

# “It'll bring hundreds of jobs.”

Our verdict
Wrong for permanent jobs.

Construction jobs are many and temporary. Operating jobs are few, often fewer than 100, and specialists often come from outside the county.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] Rural data centers tend to employ relatively few permanent workers, often fewer than 100, and many specialized services are brought in from outside the county.
Source: Futurity, reporting Georgia Tech research (July 23, 2026)

-
[PLAUSIBLE] Construction jobs are real but temporary. They end when the building is finished.

Where the critics are right
Critics who doubt the jobs number are right about permanent jobs: they are few, and specialists often come from outside the county. A county can't count on residents getting them without a plan. [PLAUSIBLE]

## What to ask for, in writing

- Local-hire targets, in writing, for construction and operations.

- Apprenticeships.

- A community college partnership, written into the agreement.

docs.title: Straight Talk #4: “It will pay for our schools.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #4 · What people say

# “It will pay for our schools.”

Our verdict
Partly right.

Data centers can carry a big share of a county's tax base. Tax abatements can give much of it away.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] In Loudoun County, Virginia, data centers generate almost 50% of property tax revenue, as reported in a trade-press review of the county's proposed fiscal 2026 budget.
Source: Data Center Frontier (Feb. 14, 2025)

-
[VERIFIED] El Paso, Texas, agreed to an 80% property tax abatement over 35 years for a $1.5 billion data center.
Source: Brookings, Turner Lee and West (Jan. 29, 2026)

-
[PLAUSIBLE] The money a school district sees depends on the abatement terms and on how state school-funding formulas treat new local revenue.

Where the critics are right
Headline tax figures can leave out abatements. If the deal gives most of the tax away, as El Paso's did, the schools may see far less than promised. [PLAUSIBLE]

## What to ask for, in writing

- Publish every abatement term before the vote.

- Publish the net revenue to each taxing district, school board first, year by year.

docs.title: Straight Talk #5: “They're 96 decibels, 24 hours a day.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #5 · What people say

# “They're 96 decibels, 24 hours a day.”

Our verdict
Overstated as a blanket claim; noise complaints are real.

Readings next to machines aren't levels at a home. But neighbors have sued over round-the-clock noise, and some cities now cap it at the property line.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] Readings taken near machines don't tell you the sound level at a property line or a home. A blanket claim of “96 decibels, 24 hours a day” is misleading; a sustained 96 dBA at a residence would be unmistakably loud and potentially hazardous.
Source: City of Linn Valley, Kansas, noise and infrasound FAQ (updated Aug. 25, 2026)

-
[VERIFIED] Neighbors in Vineland, New Jersey, have sued over round-the-clock noise from a nearby data center campus.
Source: GadgetReview (Aug. 28, 2026)

-
[VERIFIED] The City of Sanford, North Carolina, changed its development rules in April 2026 so data centers may not exceed 65 dBA at the edge of their property.
Source: NC Newsline (July 15, 2026)

Where the critics are right
Noise is a real problem for some neighbors, enough to bring a lawsuit in Vineland. And a standard decibel (dBA) reading can understate low-frequency sound (Linn Valley FAQ, above). [VERIFIED]

## What to ask for, in writing

- A dBA limit at the property line, written into the ordinance.

- Low-frequency sound measured, not just dBA.

- Setbacks, and limits on generator test hours.

- Independent, third-party monitoring.

docs.title: Straight Talk #6: “AI already uses most of America's electricity.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #6 · What people say

# “AI already uses most of America's electricity.”

Our verdict
Wrong nationally; the local share is what matters.

Data centers used 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023. But they cluster, so one utility's share can be far larger.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] U.S. data centers used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's range for 2028 is 6.7% to 12%, nearly a factor of two, because no one knows how fast AI will grow.
Source: Shehabi et al. (2024), United States Data Center Energy Usage Report, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

-
[VERIFIED] Nearly half of U.S. data center capacity sits in five regional clusters.
Source: International Energy Agency (2025), Energy and AI. Cited from the Grid & Grain library; the IEA page would not load for our recheck on Nov. 26, 2026.

Where the critics are right
A few percent nationally can be a large share of one utility's peak demand. Where one project would be a big part of the local load, the local numbers are what matter. [PLAUSIBLE]

## What to ask for, in writing

- Ask your utility or co-op what share of its peak demand the project would be.

docs.title: Straight Talk #7: “There's nothing we can do; they'll build anyway.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #7 · What people say

# “There's nothing we can do; they'll build anyway.”

Our verdict
Wrong.

States, co-ops, and counties are setting terms, and some are saying no. Zoning, tariffs, benefit agreements, and co-op elections are all levers.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] As of May 2026, 23 states had approved at least one large-load tariff.
Source: Columbia Law School, Sabin Center for Climate Change Law (June 2, 2026), citing the Edison Electric Institute

-
[VERIFIED] In August 2026, Arizona regulators unanimously approved a process for six electric co-ops that makes large-load customers cover all the costs of serving them, including new transmission, so existing members don't subsidize them.
Source: Arizona Corporation Commission (Aug. 13, 2026)

-
[VERIFIED] In Frederick County, Maryland, a developer offered $110 million in community benefits in exchange for an eight-year freeze on zoning changes that could affect its campus. After public comment, the county executive rejected the agreement on Sept. 14, 2026, and extended a moratorium on new data center applications to July 1, 2027.
Source: WYPR (Sept. 15, 2026); Maryland Association of Counties (Sept. 2, 2026)

Where the critics are right
Deals are often negotiated behind closed doors (Straight Talk #10), and having levers doesn't mean they're easy to pull. [PLAUSIBLE] Frederick County said no only after residents spoke up.

## What to ask for, in writing

- Learn which levers your county holds: zoning, permits, abatements, benefit agreements.

- Learn your co-op's: board elections, large-load tariffs, member meetings.

Correction. Corrected Nov. 26, 2026. This entry earlier said Frederick County “negotiated more than $110 million in developer-funded benefits.” The agreement was announced Sept. 1, 2026, but the county executive rejected it on Sept. 14.

docs.title: Straight Talk #8: “AI does nothing for rural people.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #8 · What people say

# “AI does nothing for rural people.”

Our verdict
Wrong, but adoption is thin.

AI tools are already easing the load on doctors at some rural hospitals. But few rural hospitals use them yet.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] At Central Montana Medical Center, a 25-bed critical access hospital, ambient AI scribing cut physicians' after-hours charting so much that some said they would consider leaving if the tool were taken away.
Source: Becker's Hospital Review (Aug. 3, 2026)

-
[PLAUSIBLE] Becker's reports that just 8% of critical access and rural community hospitals have put AI-driven predictive analytics in place. It doesn't name the survey behind the figure, so treat it as a rough size, not a measurement.
Source: Becker's Hospital Review (Aug. 3, 2026)

Where the critics are right
A data center down the road doesn't, by itself, put AI tools in the local clinic. [PLAUSIBLE] And adoption is thin: 8% is not many hospitals.

## What to ask for, in writing

- Tie any local data center deal to broadband for the hospital and schools.

- Ask for AI-readiness funding or training for the hospital and schools as part of a benefit agreement.

Correction. Corrected Nov. 26, 2026. This entry earlier graded the 8% figure VERIFIED. Becker's names no survey behind it, so it is now PLAUSIBLE.

docs.title: Straight Talk #9: “Data center power use will double forever.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #9 · What people say

# “Data center power use will double forever.”

Our verdict
Plan in ranges.

Efficiency once kept data center power use nearly flat while computing grew. AI changed that, and forecasts now span almost a factor of two.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] From 2010 to 2018, global data center electricity use rose only about 6% while computing grew about 6.5 times, because efficiency improved so fast.
Source: Masanet et al. (2020), “Recalibrating global data center energy-use estimates,” Science

-
[VERIFIED] AI broke that balance. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's 2028 projection for U.S. data centers runs from 6.7% to 12% of U.S. electricity.
Source: Shehabi et al. (2024), Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory

Where the critics are right
Growth is real. A utility that plans only for the low case can be caught short, and one that plans only for the high case can overbuild and bill members for it. [PLAUSIBLE]

## What to ask for, in writing

- Low, base, and high demand scenarios in any utility plan.

- Who pays if the high case doesn't happen.

docs.title: Straight Talk #10: “These deals are done in secret.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #10 · What people say

# “These deals are done in secret.”

Our verdict
Often right.

Local officials and residents have been asked to sign nondisclosure agreements, and secrecy is a leading driver of opposition.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] Local officials and residents have been asked to sign nondisclosure agreements about proposed projects, and a political scientist at Washington University in St. Louis describes closed-door negotiation as one of the drivers of opposition.
Source: Iowa Public Radio, Edgell (Sept. 2, 2026)

Where the critics are right
They're right. Deals are often negotiated behind closed doors, and that secrecy feeds opposition (Iowa Public Radio, above). [VERIFIED]

## What to ask for, in writing

- A transparency clause: the end user named before any vote.

- A public hearing before any vote.

- No nondisclosure agreements for elected officials.

docs.title: Straight Talk #11: “Data centers can never cut back.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #11 · What people say

# “Data centers can never cut back.”

Our verdict
Overstated.

Some can, some of the time, and the contract has to say how much.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] One operator has put 1 gigawatt of data center demand response into long-term contracts with five utilities: Indiana Michigan Power, the Tennessee Valley Authority, Entergy Arkansas, Minnesota Power, and DTE Energy. That is the company's own announcement.
Source: Google (Mar. 19, 2026)

-
[VERIFIED] Texas law now requires new customers that connect at transmission voltage after 2025 to install equipment that lets their load be cut off during an emergency, and sets up a paid program for customers of 75 megawatts or more to cut back on notice.
Source: Texas Senate Research Center, bill analysis of S.B. 6 (Aug. 5, 2025)

Where the critics are right
The same operator says there are limits to how flexible a data center can be, that the capability is available only at certain locations, and that it shifts only a portion of its workloads (Google, above). [VERIFIED] And a hall can meet a promise to cut its grid use by running diesel generators instead of using less. [PLAUSIBLE]

## What to ask for, in writing

- Megawatts: how much load the customer will drop.

- Hours per year: how often it can be called.

- The method: pausing work, batteries, or generators.

- Who meters it, and who can read the meter.

- The penalty for breaking the promise.

docs.title: Straight Talk #12: “My farm data is mine automatically.”
docs.text:
Straight Talk · #12 · What people say

# “My farm data is mine automatically.”

Our verdict
It depends on what you signed.

Industry principles say farmers own their data, but principles aren't law. The agreement you sign decides who can collect, use, share, and keep it.

## What the evidence shows

-
[VERIFIED] Farm groups and technology companies agreed on principles in 2015 that say farmers own the information generated on their operations. Ohio State University Extension describes these as guiding principles, and advises that ownership and control are set by explicit contracts, leases, and agreements. Ownership can be unclear when a landowner, a tenant, and a custom applicator share a field.
Source: Ohio State University Extension, Fulton, Port & Colley (Feb. 9, 2018)

Where the critics are right
Farmers' distrust of how their data is collected and managed is real enough that federal auditors list data sharing and ownership as one of three main barriers to precision agriculture, with high costs and a lack of standards. [VERIFIED] (GAO-24-105962, Jan. 31, 2024 )

## What to ask for, in writing

- Who can see the data, and why.

- Whether it can be sold or shared.

- Whether you can take it to another company.

- What gets deleted when you leave.

docs.title: Field Guide Module 1: The Wire to Your Porch
docs.text:
Field Guide · Module 1 of 12 · January 2027

# The Wire to Your Porch

Before anyone asks your county to vote on a data center, here’s how power gets to your porch, and why that’s the whole story.

The decision it serves: understanding your co-op or utility before anyone asks you to vote. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 19 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Making electricity and delivering electricity are two different jobs, and the grid has to balance supply and demand every second.

## Rung 1. Electricity is a delivery business

Most power plants make electricity by spinning a magnet inside coils of wire. Solar panels make it when sunlight knocks electrons loose. Either way, it then has to travel, sometimes hundreds of miles, to reach you. The poles and wires along your road are that delivery network.

So there are two jobs, and often two businesses: one that makes power and one that delivers it.

And one strange rule. Electricity is hard to store in bulk, so plants must make almost exactly as much as everyone uses, at every moment. When you flip on a light, somewhere a generator works a little harder.

AnalogyPicture your town’s water system: a pumping station, big mains, small pipes to each house, your faucet.

Where it breaksA water tower holds water for days. The grid’s wires hold almost none. The grid is less like a water tower and more like a juggler who has to catch every ball the moment it drops.

## Rung 2. Why the grid runs at 500,000 volts

Three words do most of the work. Voltage is the push. Current is the flow. Power is the two multiplied: P = V × I.

Wires resist current and turn some energy into heat, and that heat grows with the current squared. Cut the current in half and the loss drops to a quarter.

So the grid plays a trick. To move 100 megawatts at 100,000 volts takes 1,000 amps. At 500,000 volts it takes 200 amps, one fifth as much, and the heat lost on the same wire falls to one twenty-fifth.

That’s why power is stepped up at the plant, carried on tall transmission lines, stepped down at a substation, and stepped down once more by the can on your pole or the green box in your yard. Even so, about 5% of U.S. electricity is lost along the way (EIA, 2018–2022 average). [VERIFIED]

Field Test: see it in your kitchenPlug a $25 watt meter into an outlet near your microwave and read the volts. Start the microwave and watch the reading drop a few volts. Volts lost times amps flowing equals watts turned into heat in the wires between your outlet and the transformer on the pole, most of it in the wires inside your walls. A typical 1,200-watt microwave draws about 10 amps, so a 3-volt drop means about 30 watts warming the wiring. Same physics as the grid, on your counter. Plug-in meters only. Never open an outlet or a panel.

Field Test video. One outlet, one circuit, one day; readings reported as measured. Plug-in meters only.

## Rung 3. Built for the worst hour

The grid is planned to survive the hottest afternoon and the coldest morning of the year, and to keep running if its single largest piece fails. The result: much of it sits idle most of the time. Across U.S. balancing areas from 2016 to 2024, average demand was about 53% of peak (Duke University). [VERIFIED]

That empty half matters. A Duke study estimated that if large new customers agreed to cut back during the grid’s few worst hours, about 0.5% of the year, the U.S. could absorb roughly 98 gigawatts of new load without building for a new peak. [VERIFIED] as a system-wide estimate. The catch, which the authors note too: room on the whole system isn’t room at your local substation, and not every computer job can pause.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs explain how the grid works. The next two explain why it behaves the way it does when someone big asks to plug in. They get more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them and you’ll follow the conversation at your co-op’s annual meeting.

## Rung 4. How utilities earn money

The company that delivers your power is usually a monopoly: one set of wires per road, because building two would waste money. A monopoly can’t be left to set its own prices, so someone else sets them. Who that is depends on who owns the wires.

### Investor-owned utilities: paid on what they build

An investor-owned utility is a company with shareholders. A state public utility commission sets its prices in a public proceeding called a rate case. The commission adds up two things the utility needs to collect from customers:

- Operating costs: fuel, crews, trucks, billing. The utility gets these back, but makes no profit on them.

- A return on its rate base. The rate base is the value of everything the utility has built and still owns (poles, wires, substations, power plants), minus wear. The commission lets the utility earn a set percentage on that value.

In shorthand, revenue needed = operating costs + (allowed return × rate base) (National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Sept. 2015). [VERIFIED]

How big is that allowed return? In rate cases decided in the first half of 2026, regulators let electric utilities earn an average of 9.84% on the shareholders’ share of the investment, the same average as in 2025 (S&P Global Market Intelligence, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] That’s a ceiling the utility is allowed to aim for, not a guaranteed paycheck.

Look at what the formula rewards. A dollar spent on fuel comes back as a dollar. A dollar spent on a new substation comes back with a return on top, for as long as it’s on the books. So an investor-owned utility has a built-in reason to favor building things. [PLAUSIBLE] That isn’t a scandal; it’s how the system was designed to attract money for long-lived equipment. It’s why the commission, and the public at rate-case hearings, have to ask whether each project is needed and who should pay for it.

### Co-ops: owned by the people on the line

A rural electric co-op works differently. It’s a nonprofit owned by its members, who elect the board on a one-member, one-vote basis. When a co-op takes in more than it costs to run, those margins are credited back to members based on how much power each one bought. These are called capital credits, and the co-op holds the money for a period of years before paying it out (University of Wisconsin Center for Cooperatives). [VERIFIED]

So a co-op has no shareholders to reward for building. But it still borrows to build, and the members still repay that debt through their bills. If a co-op builds a substation for one giant customer and that customer leaves early, the remaining members can be left holding the loan. [PLAUSIBLE] That risk is the reason for large-load tariffs, the rules that make a big new customer prepay, sign a long contract, or post collateral. Module 2 covers them line by line.

### Where the power itself is bought

Your utility or co-op may not make the electricity it delivers. In much of the country, power is bought in a regional wholesale market. The grid operator takes offers from power plants and runs the cheapest ones first, adding more expensive plants as demand climbs. The last plant needed to meet demand sets the price, and every plant running that hour gets paid that price (ISO New England). [VERIFIED]

That’s why a big new load matters most where supply is already tight: it can push demand up to a costlier plant, and that higher price applies to every megawatt-hour in that hour. [PLAUSIBLE] It’s also why studies of data centers and power bills find the effects concentrated in tight markets such as PJM, a large regional grid operator in the East (E&E News, in Straight Talk #1). [VERIFIED]

AnalogyAn investor-owned utility is paid like the owner of a toll road who earns a fee on every mile of road built, not on every car that drives it. Building more road raises the owner’s income, so someone has to check that the road is needed.

Where it breaksA toll-road owner sets the toll. A utility’s return is set by a regulator in public, and you can testify. And a co-op is a road owned by the drivers: there’s no outside owner to enrich, but the drivers pay off the road together.

## Rung 5. Why connecting to the grid now takes years

Rung 3 showed that the grid has room most of the year. So why do new power plants and big new customers wait years to connect? Because “room on average” isn’t the question the grid asks. It asks: on the worst hour, at this exact spot, with this new thing added, does anything overload? Answering that for every request takes engineering studies, and the line for those studies is long.

### The line for new power plants

Every new power plant or battery that wants to connect to the high-voltage grid files an interconnection request and waits in an interconnection queue while the grid operator studies what upgrades it would trigger and who pays. At the end of 2025, about 2,061 gigawatts of generation and storage sat in those queues, down 10% from a year earlier. Projects that came online in 2025 took a median of 61 months, about five years, from request to operation. Of everything that asked to connect from 2000 to 2020, only 13% of the capacity had been built by the end of 2025; 75% had withdrawn (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Queued Up, 2026 edition, June 2026). [VERIFIED]

Those numbers explain each other. Filing was cheap, so developers filed many speculative requests. Requests were studied one at a time, first come, first served. And when a project ahead in line dropped out, the upgrades and costs for everyone behind it could change, so studies had to be redone.

On July 28, 2023, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) issued Order No. 2023 to fix that. It replaced one-at-a-time studies with cluster studies that look at a batch of requests together, and changed the rule from “first come, first served” to “first ready, first served.” Developers now pay study deposits, must show they control the land, and can owe a penalty for withdrawing late. Grid operators that miss study deadlines can owe penalties too (FERC). [VERIFIED]

Is it working? The queue shrank in 2025, with more than 750 gigawatts of requests withdrawn that year (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, July 2026). [VERIFIED] Whether that means faster connections, or just a shorter line with the same slow studies, is not yet settled. [PLAUSIBLE]

### The line for hardware

Even an approved connection needs equipment, and transformers, the devices that step voltage up and down, are scarce. Wood Mackenzie projected that U.S. supply would fall short of demand in 2025 by 30% for large power transformers and 10% for the distribution transformers like the one on your pole (Wood Mackenzie, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED] A project can clear the study line and still wait in the factory line.

### The line for big new customers

Data centers and other large loads wait in a separate line that the national queue reports don’t count. Texas shows how long it can get: its large-load queue held 474 gigawatts, more than five times the state grid’s summer peak of a little over 90 gigawatts (Utility Dive, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED] Much of that will never be built; some developers file the same project with several utilities to see who answers first. Texas now requires large-load applicants to show site control, cover much of their grid upgrade cost, disclose duplicate requests, and accept curtailment during emergencies (Texas Senate Bill 6, as reported by Utility Dive, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED] One industry group puts typical large-load waits at one to five years with regulated utilities and eight or more in parts of PJM (Power for Tomorrow, as reported by Utility Dive). [PLAUSIBLE] as an advocacy group’s estimate.

### Why this matters at the county line

A long line is leverage. A developer who wants to connect sooner has reasons to accept terms: pay for its own upgrades, agree to cut back during the grid’s worst hours (the flexibility from Rung 3), or bring its own batteries. When someone says a project must be approved quickly, it’s fair to ask where it actually sits in the utility’s line, what upgrades it triggers, and who pays for them.

AnalogyThe queue is the line of grain trucks at the elevator at harvest. Each truck has to be weighed and graded before it can unload, and the scale is the slow part.

Where it breaksAt the elevator, a truck that pulls out of line just makes the line shorter. In an interconnection queue, a project that drops out can change the upgrades, and the bill, for every project behind it. That’s why the new rules charge for leaving late.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Will cluster studies shorten the wait, or just move the bottleneck to transformers and transmission lines? How much of the large-load line is real? And if large loads agreed to flex at peak, how much faster could a rural substation say yes? Nobody has settled these yet. Questions for researchers, and for your utility.

## Straight Talk

“AI already uses most of America’s electricity.”

Wrong nationally. Right to watch locally.

U.S. data centers used about 4.4% of U.S. electricity in 2023 (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory). The lab’s 2028 range is 6.7% to 12%. That range is nearly a factor of two because nobody knows how fast AI will grow. [VERIFIED]

Here’s what matters for a rural county: nearly half of U.S. data center capacity sits in five regional clusters (International Energy Agency). A few percent nationally can be a big share of one utility’s system.

Ask for it in writing: what share of your utility’s or co-op’s peak demand would a proposed project be?

## Your co-op is yours

If you’re served by a rural electric co-op, you’re an owner. Co-ops own about 42% of U.S. distribution lines, covering about three-quarters of the land, and members elect the board. [VERIFIED]

That’s the most wire per customer of any kind of utility, which is why one giant new customer can change a co-op’s whole system. It’s also why member-owners have real say. Some co-ops already require big loads to prepay for the substations and lines they need.

Annual meeting season starts in February. Find your co-op’s date and put it on the calendar. Module 2, Who Pays for the Substation?, gives you the questions to bring.

Why do my lights blink two or three times in a storm and then come back?

“You just watched a recloser work. It’s a switch out on the line that acts like a smart breaker. When a branch touches a wire, it opens, waits a moment, and tries again. Field Guide · Module 2 of 12 · February 2027

# Who Pays for the Substation?

A big new customer needs a substation built before it uses a single kilowatt-hour. Here’s who pays for it, and the six lines of fine print that decide whether it’s them or you.

The decision it serves: commenting on a large-load tariff, and knowing what to ask at your co-op’s annual meeting. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 21 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Wires earn a return on capital, which rewards building. A large-load tariff decides who pays if the building outlasts the customer.

## Rung 1. Somebody always pays for the substation

Module 1 ended with a question: when one giant customer plugs in, who pays for the equipment it needs? This module answers it.

A data center can’t just plug into the line on your road. It needs its own substation, heavier lines to feed it, and sometimes upgrades farther up the grid. All of that gets built before the customer uses a single kilowatt-hour.

Your co-op or utility pays for that equipment up front, usually with borrowed money, and earns it back a little at a time through monthly bills over many years. If the big customer stays and pays, the plan works. If it leaves early, shrinks, or never shows up at all, the equipment and the loan are still there, and the cost lands on everyone else’s bills. [PLAUSIBLE]

So the real question isn’t whether a data center pays its power bill. It’s who is on the hook for what was built for it.

AnalogyTen neighbors share a gravel road and split the upkeep. A new neighbor wants the road paved a mile out to his place, on a 20-year loan in everyone’s name. He promises his share will cover it.

Where it breaksIf he moves away, a paved road still helps whoever buys his place. A substation sized for one giant customer may have no second customer in the county big enough to use it.

## Rung 2. The large-load tariff: six terms

A tariff is a utility’s published rulebook: the rates and conditions for each kind of customer. A large-load tariff is the chapter written for the biggest customers. It sets what they pay and the conditions for connecting to the grid (Columbia Law School, Sabin Center, June 2026). [VERIFIED]

As of May 2026, 23 states had approved at least one large-load tariff, and 7 more had one pending (Edison Electric Institute, as cited by the Sabin Center). [VERIFIED]

The good ones share six terms. Each one closes a different way the cost could slide onto you.

### 1. A separate rate class

Big customers are billed in their own group, so their costs don’t blend into the rates for homes and farms. Ohio’s regulators ordered the utility AEP Ohio to create a data center class for new loads above 25 megawatts (Public Utilities Commission of Ohio order of July 9, 2025, as reported by POWER magazine). [VERIFIED]

### 2. A minimum bill

The customer pays for most of the capacity it reserved, whether it uses it or not. In Ohio that floor is as high as 85% of the capacity the data center signed up for (POWER magazine, July 2025). [VERIFIED] Reserve 100 megawatts, use 40, and the bill is still figured on 85.

### 3. Collateral

The customer posts money or a bank guarantee that the utility keeps if the customer fails. Dominion Energy’s tariff in Virginia asks for $1.5 million for each megawatt of capacity (Sabin Center, June 2026). [VERIFIED]

### 4. An exit fee

Leaving early costs money. In Ohio a data center can’t buy its way out at all in the early years, and when it can, the fee equals three years of minimum charges (Vorys law firm summary of the order, July 2025). [VERIFIED]

### 5. A long contract

The contract should run closer to the life of the equipment. Ohio’s runs up to 12 years, counting a ramp-up period of up to four. Dominion’s minimum is 14. And they’re getting longer: tariffs proposed before 2025 averaged a minimum of about 5 years, and those proposed since average about 12 (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the Brattle Group, as reported by Utility Dive, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

### 6. Upgrades paid up front

The customer pays for its own substation and lines before construction, instead of the utility borrowing for them. Rappahannock Electric Cooperative in Virginia collects about 60% of a substation’s projected cost within about ten business days of signing (CoBank, Jan. 2026). [VERIFIED]

Do these terms change anything? After Ohio’s tariff took effect, AEP Ohio’s forecast of large-load demand reportedly fell by about half (Sabin Center, June 2026). [PLAUSIBLE] as a reported figure. The likely reason: projects that were only testing the water left the line once a real commitment was required.

Field Test: what one dishwasher cycle costs, twiceA minimum bill is about one idea: power costs more at some hours than others, and reserved capacity costs money even when it sits unused. See the first half at home. If your dishwasher plugs into an outlet you can reach, plug a watt meter between them, reset it, and run one normal cycle. Read the kilowatt-hours. Then find two numbers on your co-op’s rate sheet: its on-peak and off-peak price per kilowatt-hour, if it offers a time-of-use rate. Multiply. Say the cycle used 1.2 kilowatt-hours, and your rates were 16 cents on-peak and 8 cents off-peak: that’s 19 cents at suppertime and 10 cents at bedtime, for the same clean dishes. Those are example numbers, not yours. Hardwired dishwasher, or the plug is out of reach? Use the washing machine instead. Plug-in meters only. Never open an appliance, an outlet, or a panel.

Field Test video. One appliance, one cycle, one co-op’s rates; readings reported as measured. Plug-in meters only.

## Rung 3. Where you get a say

Who writes the tariff depends on who owns the wires (Module 1, Rung 4).

If you’re on a co-op, the board you elect sets the terms, sometimes with a state commission’s approval. Co-ops are already acting. In South Carolina, Central Electric Power Cooperative, which supplies 19 local co-ops, adopted a rate for loads of 20 megawatts or more: contracts of at least 15 years with penalties for leaving early, cash deposits or letters of credit, monthly minimums, and advance payment for upgrades (NRECA RE Magazine, July 2026). [VERIFIED] In Arizona, regulators voted unanimously on August 12, 2026, to approve a process for the state’s wholesale co-op and five local co-ops. Every large-load agreement gets checked to make sure no other group of customers subsidizes it (Arizona Corporation Commission, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

If you’re on an investor-owned utility, the state utility commission decides, in a public case that takes written comments. Few local voices show up. The Sabin Center reports that no city took part in Pennsylvania’s large-load proceeding (June 2026). [PLAUSIBLE] as a reported account. A county or town that files a comment is often the only local government in the record.

Where the critics are right. A tariff protects you from the cost of wires built for one customer. It doesn’t cover everything. A large new load also buys power from the same regional market you do, and where supply is tight, that can raise the price for everyone. Studies find those effects concentrated in tight markets such as PJM, the grid operator for much of the East (E&E News, in the Straight Talk library). [VERIFIED] Rung 5 explains why. A good tariff is necessary. It isn’t the whole answer.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs give you the six terms and where to ask for them. The next two explain how a rate is built in the first place, and why a tariff can protect your co-op’s books and still not shield your region’s power price. They’re more technical, but every term is defined. You can pass the self-check without them.

## Rung 4. How a rate gets built

Rates aren’t picked. They’re worked out in three steps, and each step is a place where costs can be pointed at one group of customers or another.

### Step one: how much money in total

The utility adds up what it needs to collect in a year. That total is the revenue requirement: operating costs, plus the return on what it has built (Module 1, Rung 4). For a co-op, it’s operating costs plus loan payments and a margin the lenders require.

### Step two: who caused which costs

A cost-of-service study splits that total among groups of customers, called rate classes: residential, commercial, industrial, and so on. It works in three moves. First, sort every cost by job: making power, moving it long distance, delivering it locally, serving customers. Second, label each cost by what drives it: the amount of energy used, the size of the peak, or simply the number of customers. Third, hand each class its share (South Carolina Office of Regulatory Staff, Electric Ratemaking Fundamentals, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED]

The idea underneath is cost causation: whoever causes a cost should pay it. A separate rate class for large loads is cost causation made visible. Without it, a substation built for one customer sits in a shared pool, and the study spreads it across everyone in the class.

### Step three: how the bill is shaped

Last, each class’s share is turned into prices. Most bills have two or three parts: a fixed customer charge, an energy charge per kilowatt-hour, and for larger customers a demand charge based on their highest draw (South Carolina Office of Regulatory Staff, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED] A minimum bill is a floor under the demand charge. That’s the 85% in Ohio.

### Why a big customer can push your rate either way

Here’s the part both sides of the argument get half right. Much of a utility’s cost is fixed. Spread a fixed cost over more kilowatt-hours and the price per kilowatt-hour falls. A study led by the Electric Power Research Institute found that from 2015 to 2024, a doubling of data center capacity lowered residential prices by about 4%. [VERIFIED] But a big customer also triggers new costs. A Wharton and Harvard Business School paper attributes about 4% of the rise in residential prices from 2020 to 2025 to data centers, and 15% of the rise in industrial prices. [VERIFIED] Both are in the Straight Talk library.

Those findings don’t contradict each other. Which way your bill moves depends on whether the new customer pays more than the new costs it causes. [PLAUSIBLE] The six terms are how you make sure it does.

AnalogyA big table at a restaurant can split the check evenly or by what each person ordered. Cost causation is splitting by what you ordered. A large-load tariff makes the guest who ordered the steak pay for the steak, and leave a deposit in case he walks out.

Where it breaksAt a restaurant you can see who ordered what. On a grid, one substation, one line, and one power plant serve many customers at once, so the split depends on formulas that reasonable people argue over. That argument is the rate case.

## Rung 5. Why a tariff can’t cover everything

A tariff governs the deal between one utility and one customer. The price of the power itself is set somewhere else, and by location.

### Power has a price at every point on the map

In regions with a wholesale market, the grid operator posts a price at thousands of points on the grid. It’s called the locational marginal price, and it has three parts: the cost of making the power, the cost of congestion, and the cost of power lost as heat on the lines (PJM Interconnection, Jan. 2025). [VERIFIED]

Congestion is the one to watch. When demand is low, power flows freely and prices are close to the same everywhere. As demand climbs, some lines reach the limit of what they can safely carry. The cheapest power can’t get through, so the operator runs costlier plants on the near side of the bottleneck, and the price there goes up (PJM Interconnection, Jan. 2025). [VERIFIED]

Now put a very large load on the crowded side of a bottleneck. It pays the higher price, and so does every other buyer at that spot, including your co-op’s power supplier. [PLAUSIBLE] No clause in the data center’s contract with its utility changes that, because the price comes from the market, not the contract.

### How big the requests are

Scale is what makes this matter. Rappahannock Electric Cooperative’s ordinary peak demand is about 1,150 megawatts. The requests it has received from data centers add up to about 20,000 megawatts, roughly 17 times its peak, with about a fifth of that under contract (CoBank, Jan. 2026). [VERIFIED] The co-op buys the power for those loads through a separate affiliate, so the supply costs stay off its existing members’ bills (CoBank, Jan. 2026). [VERIFIED] That’s a seventh term some co-ops now add: a separate power supply.

### Bring your own power

A newer tool goes after the supply side directly. A clean transition tariff makes the large customer responsible for bringing new generation onto the grid to match its load, the way a long-term power contract would. A proposed agreement between Google and Xcel Energy in Minnesota runs 15 years and includes a minimum monthly bill, credit support, and an exit fee (Sabin Center, June 2026). [VERIFIED]

AnalogyPJM itself compares location pricing to a taxi fare. In light traffic the fare is steady. In heavy traffic the same trip costs more.

Where it breaksA taxi fare goes up only for the rider in the cab. On the grid, when one very large rider crowds the road, the fare goes up for everyone traveling that road at that hour.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Is a 12-year contract long enough for equipment built to last decades? The thresholds in today’s tariffs run from under 1 megawatt to 150, so there’s no agreed line for what counts as “large.” And nobody has shown yet whether tariffs written in 2025 and 2026 will hold when the first big customer actually walks away. Questions for researchers, and for your board.

## Straight Talk

“Data centers are why my power bill went up.”

Overstated, with a real local risk.

The two best studies so far point in different directions and both find small effects: residential prices about 4% lower with a doubling of data center capacity from 2015 to 2024 (Electric Power Research Institute), and about 4% of the 2020 to 2025 residential price rise attributed to data centers (Wharton and Harvard Business School). [VERIFIED] Most of what raised bills in those years was something else.

The risk is real where supply is tight and where no tariff is in place. What happens next depends on the rules written now. [PLAUSIBLE]

Ask for it in writing: a large-load tariff with a separate rate class, a minimum bill, collateral, an exit fee, a long contract, and upgrades paid up front. Read the full entry.

## What to ask at your annual meeting

This is the part that reaches your kitchen table: the monthly bill. Co-op annual meetings run from February into spring, and members elect the board there. You don’t need to be an engineer to ask three questions.

- Does our co-op have a large-load tariff or policy? May I have a copy?

- If a large customer leaves early, who pays for the substation and lines built for it?

- Has anyone asked to connect a load of 20 megawatts or more, and what share of our peak would it be?

One thing people get wrong: “Co-ops have to take any customer.” Partly true. In Virginia, state law gives a co-op an obligation to serve, even where the community opposes the project (CoBank, Jan. 2026). [VERIFIED] But a duty to serve is not a duty to serve at everyone else’s expense. The co-op sets the terms. That’s what the tariff is for. The rule differs by state, so ask your co-op which one applies to you.

County Kit · Module 2

Large-load tariff checklist

The six terms on one page, each with the question to ask. Hold a draft tariff or contract next to it and check what’s covered. For a co-op meeting, a commission comment, or a county hearing.

Open the checklistOpen the checklist

## Ask Earl

AI character

What happens if the data center leaves?

“Depends what got signed before the first pole went in. Let’s trace the wire. The co-op built a substation for that customer, and there’s a loan on it. If the contract has a minimum bill and an exit fee, the customer keeps paying or pays to get out, and if it goes broke there’s collateral to draw on. If none of that’s in there, the loan doesn’t leave with them. It stays with the members. So the time to ask is before the vote, not after. Ask for it in writing.”

Ready? Five questions.

Get 4 right to pass. Retakes are fine.

Take the self-checkTake the self-check

## Sources

Every source below was opened on Nov. 26, 2026, except the three study figures marked “Straight Talk library,” which are cited from the library’s own source check of the same date.

- Nolette, V. (June 2, 2026), “Data Center Regulation: What Local Governments Should Know about Large-Load Tariffs and Clean Transition Tariffs”, Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, Columbia Law School: definition, 23 states and 7 pending (citing the Edison Electric Institute), Dominion collateral and contract term, AEP Ohio forecast, Pennsylvania docket, clean transition tariffs.

- Public Utilities Commission of Ohio (July 9, 2025), “PUCO orders AEP Ohio to create data center specific tariff”.

- Patel, S. (July 10, 2025), “Regulator Approves AEP Ohio’s Landmark Data Center Tariff”, POWER: 25-megawatt threshold, 85% minimum, up to 12 years, four-year ramp.

- Vorys, Sater, Seymour and Pease LLP (July 2025), client alert on the AEP Ohio data center tariff: exit fee of three years of minimum charges, and when it becomes available.

- Martucci, B. (Sept. 8, 2026), “Large-load tariffs increasingly rely on upfront payments, exit fees, ramp schedules”, Utility Dive, reporting on Frick et al. (Aug. 13, 2026), Electricity Rate Designs for Large Loads: 2026 Update, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the Brattle Group: 55 tariffs reviewed, contract lengths, thresholds from under 1 to 150 megawatts.

- Viswanath, T. (Jan. 9, 2026), “Defining co-op data center service obligations”, CoBank: Rappahannock Electric Cooperative’s obligation to serve, up-front payment, peak, requests, and supply affiliate.

- NRECA RE Magazine (July 20, 2026), “G&T Focus: New Rate Protects Members as Large Loads Grow in South Carolina”.

- Arizona Corporation Commission (Aug. 13, 2026), “ACC approves measure to ensure electric cooperative customers don’t pay for large load growth”.

- South Carolina Office of Regulatory Staff (Aug. 2025), Electric Ratemaking Fundamentals: revenue requirement, cost-of-service study, rate classes, parts of a bill.

- PJM Interconnection (Jan. 29, 2025), “LMP Supports Competitive Wholesale Power Markets”, and PJM Learning Center, “Locational Marginal Pricing” (the taxi comparison).

- Straight Talk library, “Data centers are why my power bill went up”: the Electric Power Research Institute study (2015–2024), the Wharton and Harvard Business School working paper (2020–2025), and E&E News (Mar. 19, 2026).

Field Guide · Module 3 of 12 · March 2027

# Why AI Eats Power

Somebody will hand your county a number: megawatts, homes powered, a percent of the grid. Here’s why AI uses the power it does, and how to tell a solid number from a soft one.

The decision it serves: reading an energy claim critically, whether it comes from a developer, a utility, or a headline. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 18 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Chips are limited by heat, and moving data costs more than math.

## Rung 1. A computer is a heater that thinks

Inside every computer chip are billions of tiny switches. They have no moving parts; electricity flips them. A switch that’s on stands for 1, and a switch that’s off stands for 0. Everything a computer does, from a text message to an AI answer, is those switches flipping in a pattern, in step with a clock that ticks billions of times a second.

Every flip moves a tiny bit of electric charge, and moving charge takes energy. That energy doesn’t vanish. It turns into heat. One flip makes almost none. Billions of flips, billions of times a second, make a chip you can’t hold your finger on.

So here’s the first thing to carry into any hearing: nearly all the electricity that goes into a computer comes back out as heat. [PLAUSIBLE] as plain physics; energy has to go somewhere, and a computer doesn’t lift, light, or move anything. A building full of computers is a building full of heaters, and that’s why Module 4 is about cooling.

AnalogyA computer is an electric space heater that does arithmetic on the way. Plug in 1,000 watts of computers and you’ve plugged in a 1,000-watt heater.

Where it breaksA space heater is supposed to get hot. A chip is ruined by heat, so every watt it makes has to be carried away at once, and that carrying takes more electricity.

## Rung 2. Voltage is the master dial

What decides how much power a chip burns? Two dials matter most: how fast the clock ticks, and how hard the electricity is pushed, which is the voltage. A chip’s power use rises in step with its clock speed, and with its voltage squared (National Research Council, 2011). [VERIFIED]

The squaring is the whole story. To run a clock faster, a chip needs a little more voltage. Push a clock 60% faster with about 12% more voltage, and the power doesn’t go up 60%. It doubles: 1.125 × 1.125 × 1.6 is about 2. [VERIFIED] by arithmetic.

For decades, chipmakers dodged that bill. Each time they made switches smaller, they lowered the voltage too, so chips got faster without getting hotter. Around 2004 that stopped working: voltage couldn’t go lower, and faster clocks meant more heat than a chip could shed. Before 2004, processor performance grew about 100 times per decade. After, a single processor was forecast to improve only about 2 times per decade (National Research Council, 2011). [VERIFIED]

The industry’s answer was to stop making one fast worker and start putting many workers on each chip. That’s where AI chips come from: thousands of small workers side by side, all doing simple math at once.

You already own proof that heat is the limit. When a processor gets too hot, it slows its own clock to protect itself. Intel calls it throttling (Intel, reviewed Apr. 2026). [VERIFIED] Your phone does the same thing on a hot dashboard.

Field Test: watch a laptop turn watts into heatCharge a laptop to 100%, then plug its charger into a watt meter. Let it sit idle for five minutes and write down the watts. Point an infrared thermometer at the vent where the warm air comes out and write that down too. Now give it hard work for ten minutes, such as a free benchmark that loads the processor, and read both again. More watts in, hotter air out. Then try the phone version: run a free benchmark app three times in a row and watch the score fall as the phone warms. That’s throttling. The phone reading is [PLAUSIBLE], like any phone-app number. Plug-in and handheld meters only. Never open a computer, a charger, or a battery.

Field Test video. One laptop, one phone, one day; readings reported as measured. Plug-in and handheld meters only.

## Rung 3. Moving data costs more than math

You’d think the arithmetic is what uses the power. It isn’t. Most of the energy goes to fetching the numbers, not adding them.

Stanford engineers worked out the numbers for one generation of chips. Adding two numbers took a sliver of energy. Fetching a number from the computer’s main memory took 500 to 3,500 times as much, depending on the size of the number. In their words, most of the energy goes “not in computation but in moving data to and from memory” (Pedram and colleagues, Stanford University, 2016). [VERIFIED]

That’s why AI is hungry. An AI model is, at bottom, a gigantic table of numbers, often billions of them. To answer one question, the chip has to pull a great many of those numbers out of memory, multiply, and put results back, over and over. It’s a moving job more than a math job. [PLAUSIBLE]

AnalogyA cook making supper. Chopping is fast. Walking to the cellar for each onion is what takes the evening. So good kitchens keep a pantry by the stove, and good chips keep small, fast memory right next to the workers.

Where it breaksA pantry can be made bigger. Memory close to the processor is small because closeness is the scarce thing, and an AI model is far too big to fit there. Most of it stays in the cellar.

### Two facts that are both true

Each AI answer is getting cheaper. Google reports that a typical text question to its Gemini assistant used about 0.24 watt-hours in May 2025, about what a television uses in nine seconds, and that the figure fell 33-fold in a year (Google, Aug. 2025). [PLAUSIBLE]: it’s the company’s own measurement and hasn’t been checked by an outside party.

The total is going up anyway. U.S. data centers used 58 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2014 and 176 in 2023, about three times as much, with the growth since 2017 driven largely by AI servers (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Dec. 2024). [VERIFIED]

Where the critics are right. A company that tells you its chips are getting more efficient is telling the truth and leaving something out. Cheaper answers mean more questions get asked, and longer ones. Efficiency per answer and total power are different numbers. When someone gives you one, ask for the other.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs explain where the power goes. The next two are about judging a number someone hands you: why AI’s appetite grows the way it does, and the questions that separate a solid estimate from a soft one. They’re more technical, but every term is defined. You can pass the self-check without them.

## Rung 4. Train once, answer forever

AI uses power in two phases. Training is building the model: feeding it text or images for weeks on thousands of chips until its table of numbers is tuned. Inference is using it: answering one question at a time, for millions of people, for years.

### Which one uses more?

Training makes the headlines, but the evidence points the other way. One estimate puts the training of a single large model in 2025 at about 0.31 terawatt-hours, roughly 0.2% of the 155 terawatt-hours that AI-focused data centers used worldwide that year. The same review concludes it’s likely that demand is dominated by inference, not training (Our World in Data, July 2026, citing Epoch AI and the International Energy Agency). [PLAUSIBLE]: these are estimates, and the companies publish little.

That matters at the county line. A training site can sit almost anywhere there’s power, and can sometimes pause. Answering questions for the public has to happen right now, all day, and often closer to the people asking.

### Why bigger keeps winning

In 2020, researchers found that an AI model’s error falls along a predictable curve, called a power law, as you give it more of three things: a bigger model, more data, and more computing (Kaplan and colleagues, 2020). [VERIFIED] On a curve like that, each further step of improvement costs a multiple of the last one, not a fixed amount more. [PLAUSIBLE] That’s the business reason behind the building boom: as long as that curve holds, more computing buys a better product.

### Not every question costs the same

A short question is cheap. A long one isn’t. Estimates gathered in the same review run from about 0.3 watt-hours for a typical question, to about 2.5 for one with 7,500 words of input, to about 50 for a request where the AI works through many steps on its own (Our World in Data, July 2026, citing Epoch AI and the International Energy Agency). [PLAUSIBLE] So “energy per question” depends heavily on which question.

AnalogyTraining is building the grain elevator: a big job, done once. Inference is running it every day of every harvest for thirty years. Ask which one moves more grain.

Where it breaksAn elevator lasts decades. An AI model is replaced by a bigger one within a year or two, so the building never really stops.

## Rung 5. How to read a power number

Every figure you’ll be shown has soft spots in the same four places.

### Power or energy?

Megawatts measure power: how hard something pulls at one moment. Megawatt-hours measure energy: how much it used over time. A site that pulls 100 megawatts around the clock uses 100 × 8,760 hours, or 876,000 megawatt-hours, a year. Substations are sized for the megawatts. Bills and fuel follow the megawatt-hours. A claim that mixes them up, or gives only one, is incomplete.

### Nameplate or real?

The number in an application is usually the most a site could ever draw. Real use runs lower. Silicon Valley Power, a city-owned utility in California, reports that its data centers’ peak loads average only about 67% of their nameplate, the rated maximum. Sites also take several years to ramp up to full operation (Energy and Environmental Economics, Dec. 2025). [VERIFIED]

### Firm or hopeful?

Requests aren’t projects. After Ohio required data centers to pay for 85% of the capacity they asked for, requests to AEP Ohio fell from 30 gigawatts to 13 (Energy and Environmental Economics, Dec. 2025). [VERIFIED] Module 2 covers that tariff. Some developers file the same project with several utilities, which inflates the apparent demand. Ask what share of a forecast is under signed contract.

### One number or a range?

Honest forecasts come as ranges. Berkeley Lab’s estimate for U.S. data centers in 2028 runs from 325 to 580 terawatt-hours, or 6.7% to 12% of the country’s electricity (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Dec. 2024). [VERIFIED] The top is nearly double the bottom, and that’s the experts being candid. History cuts both ways, too: from 2010 to 2018, the world’s data centers did about 6.5 times the computing on only about 6% more electricity (Masanet and colleagues, 2020, in the Straight Talk library). [VERIFIED] AI broke that balance, and nobody knows whether it’s broken for good.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Will cheaper answers keep being swamped by more questions, or does demand level off? Will the curve that rewards bigger models keep holding? Could smaller models running close to home do most everyday jobs for a fraction of the power? Nobody knows yet. Which is the reason to plan in ranges and write contracts that hold up at either end.

## Straight Talk

“Data center power use will double forever.”

Plan in ranges.

From 2010 to 2018, global data center electricity rose only about 6% while computing grew about 6.5 times (Masanet and colleagues, 2020). AI broke that balance after 2017, and forecasts for 2028 now span nearly a factor of two (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory). [VERIFIED]

So “it will double forever” and “efficiency will take care of it” are both guesses. The record supports neither one alone.

Ask for it in writing: low, base, and high scenarios in any utility plan, and what gets built under each. Read the full entry.

## What one question costs at your house

People ask whether using AI at home is running up the nation’s power bill. Use Google’s own figure from August 2025: 0.24 watt-hours for a typical text question. [PLAUSIBLE] A hundred questions a day for a year comes to about 9 kilowatt-hours. At an example rate of 15 cents a kilowatt-hour, that’s about $1.30 of electricity a year.

So your own questions aren’t the issue. The issue is hundreds of millions of people asking, plus longer and harder requests, all served from buildings that cluster in a few places. That’s a question about where those buildings go and who pays for their wires, which is to say, it’s a local question. Yours.

Questions to Ask About a Power Estimate

A one-page card to hold next to any power number: power or energy, peak or average, what’s counted, nameplate or real, compared with what, and how sure.

## Ask Earl

AI character

Why does my phone get warm?

“Same reason a wire does. Electricity doing work leaves heat behind. That phone has billions of little switches in it, and every time one flips, it gives off a speck of heat. Ask it to do something hard and they’re all flipping at once. When it gets too warm it slows itself down on purpose, so it doesn’t cook. Now picture a building with thousands upon thousands of those chips running flat out, day and night. That’s a data center. The question isn’t whether it makes heat. It’s where the heat goes, and what it takes to move it.”

Ready? Five questions.

- Google (Aug. 21, 2025), “Measuring the environmental impact of AI inference”, and Elsworth et al. (2025), arXiv:2508.15734: 0.24 watt-hours per median text prompt, nine seconds of television, 33-fold reduction. Company-reported; not independently verified.

- Ritchie, H. (July 20, 2026), “How much energy do data centers and artificial intelligence use?”, Our World in Data: training versus inference; energy per query estimates.

- Kaplan, J., et al. (Jan. 23, 2020), “Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models”, arXiv:2001.08361.

Field Guide · Module 4 of 12 · April 2027

# The Water Question

“It’ll drain the aquifer” and “it uses no water at all” can both be said about the same size of building. Here’s how to find out which one you’re being offered.

The decision it serves: evaluating a water-use permit or a water claim. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 18 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Cooling design, not size, decides the water bill.

## Rung 1. Heat always runs downhill

Module 3 ended with a building full of heaters. Nearly every watt that goes into a computer comes out as heat, and a chip is ruined if that heat stays put. So the first job of a data center is moving heat from the chips to the outdoors.

Heat has one rule it never breaks: it flows from hot things to cold things, the way water runs downhill. To keep a hot computer cool, you give its heat a path to somewhere cooler and keep that path open.

At the end of that path, a building has two ways to hand its heat to the outside air. It can evaporate water, the way sweat cools your skin. Or it can blow air across a radiator, the way a truck cools its engine. The first way uses water, a lot of it. The second uses almost none, and more electricity.

That one choice is most of the water question.

AnalogyOn a hot day you cool off two ways. You sweat, which works well and costs you water. Or you stand in front of a fan, which costs no water and works less well the hotter the air gets.

Where it breaksYou drink a few quarts and you’re fine. A building that sweats takes its water from the same pipes or the same aquifer the town does, and the water it evaporates doesn’t come back down the drain.

## Rung 2. Which kind of cooling?

Before you argue about gallons, ask which of three families the project is in (Data Center Frontier, July 2026). [VERIFIED]

- Evaporative. Cooling towers and similar equipment evaporate water to carry heat away. This family uses the most water.

- Dry, or closed-loop. Liquid circulates in sealed pipes, like the coolant in a truck, and fans push the heat out through big radiators. Little or no water is used in normal running. In hot weather these systems need more electricity.

- Hybrid. Runs dry in mild weather and adds water when it’s hot. Its water use is concentrated on the hottest days.

How far apart are they? A large data center can use up to 5 million gallons a day, about what a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people uses (Environmental and Energy Study Institute, June 2025). [VERIFIED] In evaporative systems, about 80% of the water taken in evaporates (same source). [VERIFIED]

At the other end, the developer of a very large closed-loop campus in Port Washington, Wisconsin, says its peak daily water use will be less than 22,000 gallons, about what 65 homes use (Vantage Data Centers, as reported by TMJ4 News, Sept. 2025). [VERIFIED] as the company’s stated plan. It’s a promise, not yet a meter reading.

That’s a gap of more than 200 to 1, between buildings that can be the same size. So size tells you little. The cooling design tells you most of it.

Where the critics are right. Closed-loop isn’t free. It needs a first fill (about 1.2 million gallons at Port Washington, by the same report). It uses more electricity in the heat, and making electricity uses water somewhere else. Rung 4 follows that water. And a design on paper can change before the building opens, which is why the number belongs in the permit.

## Rung 3. The peak day and the pipe

A water system, like the grid, is built for its worst day. So the number that matters to your town isn’t a data center’s average use. It’s the most it will ever ask for in one day, and that day will be the hottest of the summer, when everybody else’s demand is highest too.

Engineers call the ratio of the peak day to the average day a peaking factor. For ordinary water customers taken together, it’s about 1.5 to 2.5. For data centers, one research team estimates 3 to 10 (Han and colleagues, Mar. 2026). [PLAUSIBLE]: it’s a recent study that hasn’t been through peer review. A data center that looks modest on an annual average can ask for a great deal on one July afternoon.

Meeting that peak can mean new pumps, mains, or treatment capacity. The same study lists a pump station costing $5.4 million to serve about 100,000 gallons a day, and a host town in Wisconsin facing an upgrade of more than $100 million after a request for 1.2 million gallons a day. [PLAUSIBLE] Somebody pays for that pipe. It’s the substation question from Module 2, with water in it.

So ask four things, and ask for them in the permit:

- Cooling type: evaporative, dry, or hybrid?

- Peak-day and average-day gallons, both.

- The source: city water, a well, the river, or reclaimed wastewater?

- A drought clause: what does the site cut back, and when, if the town is under water restrictions?

Field Test: when a cold glass sweatsEvaporation only cools when the air has room for more water. You can measure that room on your porch. Set a $10 digital hygrometer in the shade and read the temperature and the relative humidity. Look up the dew point for those two numbers with the National Weather Service’s free online calculator: at 77°F and 50% humidity, it’s about 57°F. Now fill a glass with ice water and take its surface temperature with an infrared thermometer. If the glass is colder than the dew point, it sweats. If it’s warmer, it stays dry. On a dry day the dew point sits far below the air temperature, and evaporative cooling works well. On a muggy day the two are close, and it works poorly, so the system runs harder. Report your own readings as measured. Handheld meters only. Never open or touch cooling equipment, yours or anyone else’s.

Field Test video. One porch, one glass, one day; readings reported as measured. Handheld meters only.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs cover the water a data center takes at the site. The next two follow the water you can’t see: the water used to make its electricity, and the gaps in what anyone measures. They’re more technical, but every term is defined. You can pass the self-check without them.

## Rung 4. The hidden water

A data center uses water in two places. Direct water is used at the site, mostly for cooling. Indirect water is used at the power plants that make its electricity, because most power plants boil water to spin a turbine and then cool that steam.

### The bigger share is upstream

A 2021 study of U.S. data centers found that about 75% of their water footprint was indirect, at power plants, and about 25% was at the site (Siddik and colleagues, 2021, as reported by Eos). [VERIFIED] Berkeley Lab’s later estimate leans even further that way: in 2023, U.S. data centers used about 66 billion liters of water on site, roughly 17 billion gallons, and nearly 800 billion liters, about 211 billion gallons, indirectly through their electricity (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Dec. 2024). [VERIFIED] That’s about twelve times as much upstream as on site.

The two studies use different methods and years, so don’t average them. Both say the same thing: most of the water is where you can’t see it, and often in someone else’s watershed.

### The trade nobody escapes

Here’s the tension. Evaporative cooling saves electricity by spending water. Dry cooling saves water by spending electricity, and cutting water at the site can shift some of the demand to the power system (Data Center Frontier, July 2026). [VERIFIED] Which trade is better depends on the local watershed and the local grid. In a dry county fed by a low-water power supply, dry cooling is plainly better. Where water is plentiful and the grid is strained on hot afternoons, the answer is less obvious. [PLAUSIBLE]

### The number to ask for

The industry’s yardstick is water usage effectiveness: liters of water used at the site for each kilowatt-hour of electricity the computers use. Lower is better, and a dry system can be close to zero. Berkeley Lab puts the U.S. average for site water at about 0.36 liters per kilowatt-hour through 2023, against about 4.5 liters per kilowatt-hour used indirectly to make the electricity (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Dec. 2024). [VERIFIED]

Like any yardstick, it has a boundary. Site water usage effectiveness leaves out the upstream water entirely. And a building can post an excellent energy score by evaporating a great deal of water. Ask for the energy number and the water number together.

AnalogyBuying a steak, you don’t see the water the cattle drank. A data center’s electric meter is like that steak: most of the water behind it was used miles away.

Where it breaksCattle water falls as rain on the pasture. Power-plant water comes from a particular river or reservoir, and a county that hosts the data center may not be the county that hosts the power plant. The hidden water has an address. It may not be yours.

## Rung 5. What nobody is measuring

You can’t manage what isn’t metered, and much of this isn’t.

### Few operators count

A review in 2021 found that fewer than a third of data center operators tracked their water use at all (Mytton, npj Clean Water, 2021). [VERIFIED] The same review put U.S. data center water consumption at about 1.7 billion liters a day, against about 1,218 billion liters a day for the whole country, a little over a tenth of one percent. [VERIFIED] That national share is small. It’s also the wrong scale: water is local, and a national average says nothing about one town’s wells.

### Evaporated water is gone from the basin

Most water a town uses goes down a drain and returns to the river after treatment. Water that’s evaporated doesn’t. One estimate is that data centers evaporate about 75% of the water they withdraw, against about 12% for public water supply on average (Han and colleagues, Mar. 2026). [PLAUSIBLE] So a gallon sold to an evaporative data center isn’t the same as a gallon sold to a neighborhood. In a basin that’s already short, that difference is the whole argument.

### The rules are starting to arrive

Lawmakers in at least six states have introduced bills requiring data centers to report water use or disclose what they expect to need. Virginia’s law takes effect January 1, 2027: certain water providers must report, every month, how much drinking water and reclaimed water they deliver to data centers (National Conference of State Legislatures, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] Tucson, Arizona, went further in August 2025. After a proposed data center there was voted down, the city moved to require a public mayor-and-council vote on any application for large water use, with the applications open as public records (KJZZ, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED]

A county doesn’t have to wait for the state. Reporting can be a condition of a permit or a water contract.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] As chips get hotter and move to liquid cooling, does site water use fall, or does the heat just get rejected through bigger evaporative systems? Can reclaimed wastewater supply most cooling without shorting the river downstream? And should a water permit count the upstream water at the power plant, when that plant is in another county? Nobody has settled these. Questions for researchers, and for your water board.

## Straight Talk

“A data center will drain our water.”

It depends on the cooling.

Large data centers can use up to 5 million gallons a day (Environmental and Energy Study Institute). A closed-loop campus planned in Port Washington, Wisconsin, says its peak will be under 22,000 gallons a day, about 65 homes (TMJ4 News). [VERIFIED] About three-quarters of the U.S. data center water footprint is upstream at power plants (Siddik and colleagues, 2021). [VERIFIED]

So the worry is reasonable, and it isn’t automatic. It turns on a design choice you can ask about before the vote.

Ask for it in writing: cooling type, peak and average gallons, the source, and a drought curtailment clause. Read the full entry.

## Your well, your water bill

Two things reach your kitchen. The first is supply. If the site draws on the same aquifer as your well or your town’s wells, what matters is how much it evaporates in a dry August, and whether its permit makes it cut back before you have to.

The second is the bill. If the water utility builds new mains, pumps, or treatment for one large customer, ask who pays: that customer up front, or every ratepayer over thirty years. The six terms from Module 2 work for water too: a separate rate class, a minimum bill, collateral, an exit fee, a long contract, and upgrades paid up front.

Your water utility’s manager knows the system’s peak-day capacity and how much of it is spoken for. That’s a public number. Ask for it.

Water Disclosure Checklist
