Open the kitOpen the kit
Download PDFDownload PDF

## Ask Earl

AI character

How does a data center stay cool?

“Same two ways you do. It can sweat, or it can stand in front of a fan. The sweating kind runs water over the heat and lets it evaporate. Works fine, but that water’s gone, and it wants the most on the hottest day of the year. The fan kind keeps its water in sealed pipes, like the radiator on a line truck, and blows the heat off with air. Hardly any water, but it pulls more power when it’s hot out. Neither one’s wrong. They’re different bills. So don’t ask how big the building is. Ask which kind it is, and get the gallons in writing.”

Ready? Five questions.

Get 4 right to pass. Retakes are fine.

Take the self-checkTake the self-check

## Sources

Every source below was opened on Nov. 26, 2026. The Siddik study was read through Eos’s report of it; the journal page itself could not be opened.

- Chernicoff, D. (July 20, 2026), “Tech Explainer: Data Center Cooling: Air, Evaporative, Liquid, and Hybrid Approaches”, Data Center Frontier: the cooling families and the energy-for-water trade.

- Yañez-Barnuevo, M. (June 25, 2025), “Data Centers and Water Consumption”, Environmental and Energy Study Institute: up to 5 million gallons a day (citing the Washington Post, Apr. 2023); about 80% evaporates; 211 billion gallons indirect in 2023.

- Gaul, A. (Sept. 19, 2025), “Neighbors concerned with water consumption as Port Washington data center construction to start next month”, TMJ4 News: peak under 22,000 gallons a day, about 65 homes; 1.2 million gallon fill.

- Han, Y., Li, P., Wierman, A., & Ren, S. (Mar. 18, 2026), “Small Bottle, Big Pipe: Quantifying and Addressing the Impact of Data Centers on Public Water Systems”, arXiv:2603.02705 (preprint): peaking factors, share evaporated, infrastructure cost examples.

- Chapman, A. (July 12, 2021), “U.S. Data Centers Rely on Water from Stressed Basins”, Eos, reporting on Siddik, Shehabi, & Marston (2021), Environmental Research Letters: 75% indirect, 25% on site.

- Shehabi et al. (Dec. 2024), 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Sections 4 and 5: 66 billion liters direct and nearly 800 billion liters indirect in 2023; 0.36 and 4.52 liters per kilowatt-hour.

- Mytton, D. (2021), “Data centre water consumption”, npj Clean Water 4, 11 (author’s copy): fewer than a third of operators track water; 1.7 of 1,218 billion liters a day.

- Ulizio, E. (Aug. 5, 2026), “3 Trends in State Regulation of Data Center Water Use”, National Conference of State Legislatures.

- KJZZ (Aug. 21, 2025), “After ousting Project Blue, Tucson adopts new city regulations for large water users”.

- Dew point figures are computed with the Magnus formula (Alduchov & Eskridge, 1996, Journal of Applied Meteorology). National Weather Service offices host free dew point calculators, for example weather.gov/lwx/calculator.

Field Guide · Module 5 of 12 · May 2027

# Noise, Light, and Land

Noise is the complaint neighbors actually live with. Here’s how sound travels, what counties are already writing into law, and how to tell a rule you can enforce from one you can’t.

The decision it serves: writing or reviewing a zoning ordinance. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 18 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

A limit at the property line beats a promise in a press release.

## Rung 1. How sound fades

Modules 3 and 4 followed the heat out of the building. Moving that heat takes fans, pumps, and chillers, and all of them make noise. So does the row of backup generators out back. A data center’s sound is mostly the sound of its cooling.

Loudness is measured in decibels. A whisper is about 30. A humming refrigerator is about 40. A normal talking voice at arm’s length is 65 to 80. Sounds at 85 or more can damage hearing over time (National Institutes of Health, citing the CDC). [VERIFIED] You’ll usually see the unit written dBA. The A means the meter is tuned to hear roughly the way a person does.

Sound fades as you walk away from it, by a fixed rule: out in the open, the level drops 6 decibels each time you double your distance from the source (Simon Fraser University acoustics handbook). [VERIFIED] for a single source with nothing reflecting the sound.

Notice what that rule does. The first doubling is cheap: from 10 feet to 20 feet. The eighth doubling is expensive: from a quarter mile to a half mile. Distance helps a lot close in and less and less farther out. That’s why where the machines sit on the property matters as much as how big the property is.

AnalogyA pebble dropped in a pond. The ripple is tall where the pebble lands and flattens as the ring spreads, because the same energy is stretched around a bigger and bigger circle.

Where it breaksA pond is flat and empty. Real sound bounces off buildings, bends over hills, carries farther on a still night, and adds up when there are a hundred machines instead of one pebble.

## Rung 2. Measure it at the property line

You’ll hear two kinds of claims. From opponents: “They’re 96 decibels, 24 hours a day.” From developers: “You won’t hear a thing.” Both skip the only question that matters: how loud, measured where?

The city of Linn Valley, Kansas, put it plainly while studying its own ordinance. Levels right next to machines or inside equipment rooms can be very high, but those readings don’t establish the level at a property line or a home (City of Linn Valley, updated Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] Next to a big generator, 100 decibels is possible. At a house a half mile off, it’s a different number. Neither number is a lie. Only one of them is about your bedroom.

So the rule worth having names a number and a place: no more than so many decibels, measured at the property line. Counties are writing these now.

- Sanford, North Carolina: data centers may not exceed 65 dBA at the perimeter of their property, and the city may order independent testing (NC Newsline, July 2026). [VERIFIED]

- Henry County, Virginia: 50 dBA at the property line, a sound study before construction, a test within 90 days of full operation, and testing every year for the life of the facility (WDBJ, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

- Spencer County, Indiana: an ordinance text posted by the county sets 50 dBA at the property line, and says that if the place is already louder than that, the data center may not add to it (Spencer County Ordinance 2026-07). [VERIFIED] as the posted text; the copy we read was unsigned.

Fifteen decibels separates 50 from 65. That’s a big gap. By the rule in Rung 1, it’s the difference between standing at one spot and standing more than five times farther away. Which number is right for your county is a local choice. What matters is that there is a number, a place it’s measured, and someone other than the operator doing the measuring.

Where the critics are right. Noise complaints are real, and a limit on paper doesn’t end them. Neighbors in Vineland, New Jersey, have sued over round-the-clock noise from a data center (in the Straight Talk library). [VERIFIED] A limit nobody tests is a press release with a number in it.

Field Test: walk away from an air conditionerOn a still day, stand 1 meter, about one long step, from your own home’s outdoor air conditioner unit while it’s running. Open a sound-meter app and write down the reading. Then read it again at 2 meters, 4 meters, and 8 meters, walking straight out into the yard. Turn the unit off at the thermostat and take the background level at the same four spots. In open ground you should lose close to 6 decibels each time you double the distance, until the reading sinks into the background. Next to a wall you’ll lose less. A phone reading is [PLAUSIBLE], never VERIFIED: the federal government’s own app claims accuracy within 2 decibels only on the phones it was tested on. Phone app only. Don’t touch, open, or reach into the unit, and measure only on your own property.

Field Test video. One air conditioner, one yard, one day; phone-app readings, graded PLAUSIBLE. Nothing opened or touched.

## Rung 3. The working parts of an ordinance

A noise number is one line. The ordinances passed in 2026 pair it with a handful of others, and each one does a job.

- Setbacks. Distance between the equipment and the neighbors. Henry County requires at least 1,000 feet from land that isn’t zoned industrial (WDBJ, Aug. 2026). Spencer County’s text requires at least 500 feet from homes and recommends 1,000 (Ordinance 2026-07). [VERIFIED] Remember Rung 1: the first few hundred feet buy the most quiet.

- Screening. Berms and evergreens along roads and neighbors’ lines. Spencer County’s text asks for a screen at least 20 feet tall once it’s grown. [VERIFIED]

- Light. Outdoor lights aimed inward and downward and shielded, so they don’t spill onto neighbors or light up the night sky (Spencer County Ordinance 2026-07). [VERIFIED]

- Generator test hours. Backup generators have to be run regularly to prove they work. Henry County limits routine testing to weekdays, 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. (WDBJ, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

- Monitoring. A sound study by an outside engineer before construction, a test after opening, and repeat testing. The operator pays.

- The end of the story. Henry County requires money set aside to cover taking the facility down someday, with the estimate reviewed every three years (WDBJ, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

All of these cost little to require before a site is designed. After the concrete is poured, moving a generator yard 500 feet is nearly impossible. [PLAUSIBLE] The time to write it down is before the vote.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs give you the limit, the place to measure, and the parts of an ordinance. The next two cover what a simple decibel number misses, and who actually has the power to enforce any of it. They’re more technical, but every term is defined. You can pass the self-check without them.

## Rung 4. The hum a meter can miss

People who live near data centers often describe a low hum or a steady tone, not a roar. A standard reading can understate both.

### Low-pitched sound

An A-weighted meter (dBA) is built to be less sensitive to low-pitched sound, because human ears are too. But big fans and engines put out a lot of low-pitched sound. A thorough study also uses C-weighting (dBC), which counts the low end more fully, or looks at each band of pitch separately (City of Linn Valley, updated Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

Spencer County’s text handles it this way: low-pitched or tonal sound may not exceed the dBC level that was there before construction (Ordinance 2026-07). [VERIFIED] That only works if someone measured the place before construction. The baseline reading is the cheapest study a county will ever commission, and it can’t be done afterward.

### A single tone

A steady whine at one pitch is more annoying than a broad whoosh at the same decibel level. [PLAUSIBLE] Henry County’s rule says equipment may not produce a clearly audible pure tone at or beyond a residential property line (WDBJ, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

### Averages and adding up

Two more traps. First, many limits are written as an average over time, called Leq. An average can hide a generator test that’s loud for one hour a week. Ask whether the limit is an average or a maximum. Second, decibels don’t add like ordinary numbers. Two identical machines aren’t twice the decibels of one; they’re 3 decibels more. Ten identical machines are 10 more. [VERIFIED] by arithmetic. So a study has to model the whole site running at once on its hottest day, not one unit.

AnalogyA bathroom scale that only weighs what’s above your knees. It gives a real number, and it’s the wrong number for the question. A dBA-only study of a low hum is that scale.

Where it breaksThe scale is simply wrong. A-weighting is right for most everyday sound, which is why it’s the standard. It just needs a second reading alongside it when the source is big, slow machinery.

## Rung 5. Who decides, and who enforces

### Zoning is local

Rates are set by a state commission or a co-op board. Land use is usually set at the county or the city. That makes zoning the lever closest to home. Henry County’s process shows the steps: a new zoning district for data centers, a rezoning with public hearings before the planning commission and the board of supervisors, and then a special use permit with its own hearing, where conditions can be added (WDBJ, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] States differ in how much they leave to local government, so check with your county attorney.

### Generators: what federal rules cover, and what they don’t

A data center keeps enough backup generators to carry its whole load through a grid outage, plus spares, so a large site can have dozens. [PLAUSIBLE] Federal air rules let an emergency engine run up to 100 hours a year for maintenance checks and readiness testing, and put no time limit on running in a real emergency (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Sept. 2013). [VERIFIED]

So “they’ll run diesel all the time” overstates it for emergency engines. But the federal rule is about air pollution, not noise, and not the time of day. One hundred hours each across dozens of engines is a lot of testing. [PLAUSIBLE] When those hours fall is left to you. That’s the weekday, 9-to-5 clause.

### Enforcement is the hard part

An ordinance is only as strong as the county’s ability to check it. A rural county rarely owns a certified sound meter or employs an acoustical engineer. The ordinances above answer that by making the operator pay for third-party testing on a schedule and after credible complaints, and by treating each day of a continuing violation as a separate offense (Spencer County Ordinance 2026-07). [VERIFIED]

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Does very low-pitched sound from large cooling plants affect health at the levels neighbors report, or mainly sleep and comfort? What happens to a 50-decibel limit when three campuses sit on adjoining parcels, each one compliant alone? And is a 1,000-foot setback enough for the larger machines now being designed? Nobody has settled these. Questions for researchers, and for your planning board.

## Straight Talk

“They’re 96 decibels, 24 hours a day.”

Overstated as a blanket claim. Noise complaints are real.

Readings taken next to machines don’t equal levels at a home (City of Linn Valley). Neighbors in Vineland, New Jersey, have sued over round-the-clock noise. Sanford, North Carolina, caps data centers at 65 dBA at the edge of the property (NC Newsline). [VERIFIED]

So don’t argue about the 96. Argue about the number at your fence.

Ask for it in writing: a dBA limit at the property line, low-frequency measurement, setbacks, generator test hours, and third-party monitoring. Read the full entry.

## At your fence line

Power bills and water tables are things you read about. Noise and light you live with, every night, at your own house. That’s why this is the module to bring to a planning board meeting.

Two things a resident can do before any project is approved. First, ask the county to commission a baseline sound reading at the nearest homes, in dBA and dBC, day and night. It’s the “before” that makes every later complaint provable. Second, ask where on the site the cooling equipment and generators will sit. The same building can be a good neighbor or a bad one depending on which side the machines face.

And if you farm or own land nearby: setbacks, screening, and shielded lights are cheap to require at the start and costly to add later. Ask for them now.

County Kit · Module 5

Model Ordinance Terms

A one-page worksheet for marking up a draft ordinance: the noise limit and where it’s measured, low-pitched sound, studies and monitoring, setbacks, light, generator test hours, and decommissioning.

Open the kitOpen the kit
Download PDFDownload PDF

## Ask Earl

AI character

How loud is 65 dBA?

“About a normal talking voice at arm’s length. Doesn’t sound like much, does it? Now picture that voice outside your bedroom window all night, every night, and it never takes a breath. That’s the difference between loud and constant. A number tells you how loud. It doesn’t tell you how long, or how low the pitch is, or whether it’s your fence they measured at. So when somebody quotes you decibels, ask three things. Measured where? Averaged or peak? And who’s holding the meter? Then ask for it in writing.”

Ready? Five questions.

Get 4 right to pass. Retakes are fine.

Take the self-checkTake the self-check

## Sources

Every source below was opened on Nov. 26, 2026, except the Vineland lawsuit, which is cited from the Straight Talk library.

- National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders, Noisy Planet: “Listen Up” sound levels (figures from the CDC): whisper, refrigerator, talking voice, the 85-decibel threshold.

- Simon Fraser University, Sonic Studio, “Inverse-Square Law”, acoustics handbook: 6 decibels per doubling of distance, for point sources in free-field conditions.

- City of Linn Valley, Kansas (updated Aug. 25, 2026), “Noise & Infrasound” FAQ: machine readings versus property-line levels; generator levels; A-weighting and dBC.

- NC Newsline (July 15, 2026), “Lee County residents demand pause on NC data center, claiming deception”: Sanford’s 65 dBA perimeter limit and third-party testing.

- WDBJ (Aug. 26, 2026), “Henry County adopts ‘stringent’ regulations on data centers”: 50 dBA, pure tones, 1,000-foot setback, generator test hours, annual testing, decommissioning assurance, the approval process.

- Spencer County, Indiana, Ordinance No. 2026-07, Data Centers (posted text; the copy opened was unsigned and undated): 50 dBA Leq, dBC baseline, 500-foot setback, screening, lighting, studies, penalties.

- U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (Sept. 19, 2013), “RICE NESHAP Requirements for Stationary Engines at Area Sources of Hazardous Air Pollutants”: 100 hours a year for maintenance and testing; no limit in emergencies.

- National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (updated Oct. 28, 2026), NIOSH Sound Level Meter app: accurate within 2 dBA in the lab; iOS only.

- Straight Talk library, “They’re 96 decibels, 24 hours a day”: the Vineland, New Jersey, lawsuit (GadgetReview, Aug. 28, 2026).

This module is general education, not legal advice. Your county attorney drafts the ordinance. Spot an error? Email ruralamerica56@gmail.com. We correct within 48 hours, in public.

Henry County, Virginia: 50 dBA at the property line, a 1,000-foot setback from non-industrial land, routine generator testing on weekdays from 9 to 5, testing every year, and money set aside for decommissioning (WDBJ, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] Sanford, North Carolina: 65 dBA at the perimeter, with third-party testing (NC Newsline, July 2026). [VERIFIED]

- Spencer County, Indiana. The examples marked “text” come from Ordinance No. 2026-07 as posted by the county. The copy we opened was unsigned, so treat it as drafted language. [VERIFIED] as the posted text.

- Generators. Federal air rules allow emergency engines up to 100 hours a year of maintenance and testing and don’t say when (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Sept. 2013). [VERIFIED] The hours are a local choice.

docs.text:
Field Guide · Module 6 of 12 · June 2027

# The Rural Hospital Runs on Compute

Your hospital is being offered AI tools. Here’s what they do, where the computing actually happens, and what has to be in place before anyone signs.

The decision it serves: choosing AI tools and the infrastructure behind them. About 12 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 20 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

The clinic is valuable because it is close. Its AI tools are only as good as the connection, the contract, and the people checking the work.

## Rung 1. The clinic is close, and its computer is far

A Critical Access Hospital is small on purpose. To earn the name it has 25 or fewer inpatient beds, sits more than 35 miles from the next hospital in most cases, keeps the average stay to 96 hours or less, and runs an emergency room around the clock. As of October 2026 there were 1,386 of them (Rural Health Information Hub, updated Nov. 2026). [VERIFIED]

What a hospital like that sells is distance. It’s the emergency room you can reach in time.

Now the hospital is being offered AI tools. The most common is an AI scribe: software that listens to a visit, with the patient’s permission, and drafts the doctor’s note. The doctor reads the draft, fixes it, and signs it.

Here is the part most people miss. The scribe almost never runs in the hospital. The sound leaves the exam room, travels over the internet to a data hall that may be several states away, and the draft note travels back. The clinic is close. Its computer is far.

So a rural hospital that buys an AI tool is really buying three things: a connection to reach it, a contract that says what happens to the recording, and a habit of checking the answers.

AnalogyThe regional medical center two hours away has every specialist. The clinic in town has one thing the big hospital can’t offer: it’s here. Computing splits the same way. A giant data hall is the regional center. A computer in the building is the clinic.

Where it breaksYou can’t move a patient in a thousandth of a second, but you can move a question. So a hospital doesn’t have to choose one or the other. The real choice, tool by tool, is which jobs go down the road and which stay in the building.

## Rung 2. What a scribe saves, and what it gets wrong

Start with what is working. At Central Montana Medical Center, a 25-bed critical access hospital in Lewistown, an AI scribe cut after-hours charting so much that some physicians said they would consider leaving if it were taken away (Becker’s Hospital Review, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] At Patterson Health Center, a 16-bed critical access hospital in Kansas, documentation time fell from 20 minutes to 12 per patient (Rural Health Information Hub, citing Healthcare IT News). [VERIFIED] as the hospital’s own report, not an independent study.

For a hospital that struggles to recruit one doctor, time back is the whole case.

Now what goes wrong. The same federally funded rural health toolkit lists the reported problems: notes that include things nobody said, missed clinical details, words pinned on the wrong speaker, and lower accuracy for patients with regional accents or who speak a language other than English. Its conclusion is plain: human review is a necessity, and that review takes back some of the time saved (Rural Health Information Hub). [VERIFIED]

Two words explain how these tools use power. Training is building the AI model, done once in a giant data hall. Inference is using it, once for every question. A scribe is inference: every visit sends a new job to a computer somewhere. Module 3 covered why that takes energy. This module asks where that computer should sit.

Field Test: words per joule on your own laptopA small AI model can run on an ordinary laptop with no internet at all. Plug the laptop into a $25 watt meter with its battery full, and read the watts while it sits idle. Then ask a free, small language model to write 300 words and time it. Watts times seconds is joules, the unit of energy. Words divided by joules is the score. You’ll see two things: the laptop draws power even when it’s doing nothing, and a small model on a modest machine is slow but real. Plug-in meters only. Never open the laptop or its charger.

Field Test video. One laptop, one model, one day; readings reported as measured. Plug-in meters only.

## Rung 3. No broadband, no AI

If the computer is far, the wire to it decides everything. Two numbers describe a connection. Speed is how much data fits through per second. Latency is how long one round trip takes: the delay between asking and hearing back. A scribe can live with a little delay. A video visit with a specialist can’t live with much.

On the federal map, rural broadband has improved. As of June 2025, 96.9% of Americans could get wired or fixed-wireless service at 100 megabits down and 20 up. In rural areas the figure was 86.7%, and 75.3% for wired service alone. More than 9 million rural Americans still had no such option (FCC, 2026 Section 706 Report, as reported by TelecomLead, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

Read that number carefully. It counts homes where a provider says service is available. It doesn’t tell you what the hospital actually receives at 7 a.m. on a Monday, or whether the building has a second line for the day the first one is cut. [PLAUSIBLE] Those are questions for the hospital’s own speed tests and its own contract.

Adoption is thin so far. Becker’s reports that just 8% of critical access and rural community hospitals have put AI-driven predictive analytics to work (Becker’s Hospital Review, Aug. 2026). [PLAUSIBLE] The article doesn’t name the survey behind the figure, so treat it as a rough size, not a measurement.

That gap is the opening for a county. When a data center developer asks for something, the fiber it brings, and whether that fiber reaches the hospital and the school, is a thing to ask for in writing.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs explain what a rural hospital is buying when it buys AI. The next two explain the engineering underneath: what one answer costs in energy, and how to decide which computing belongs in the building. They get more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them and you can sit across the table from a vendor.

## Rung 4. What one answer costs

An AI language model is a very large table of numbers, called parameters, learned during training. To answer, the computer runs your words through that table one piece at a time. Each piece of output is a token: a word or a piece of a word. Bigger models have more parameters, need more memory to hold them, and do more arithmetic per token.

### Energy is power times time

The energy for one answer is the power the machine draws multiplied by how long the answer takes. A watt is a rate. A joule is one watt for one second. A watt-hour is 3,600 joules.

Here is a worked example, not a measurement. Suppose a laptop draws 40 watts while a small model writes 300 words in 30 seconds. That’s 40 watts × 30 seconds = 1,200 joules, or a third of a watt-hour. The score is 300 words ÷ 1,200 joules = 0.25 words per joule. The Field Test gives you the real numbers for your own machine.

Now subtract the idle draw. If that laptop pulls 10 watts just sitting there, only 30 of the 40 watts were the model’s doing. A computer that is switched on spends energy whether or not it is working. In a hospital, a server that waits all night for the morning’s first patient is paying that idle bill the whole time. [PLAUSIBLE]

### What the big halls report

For comparison, Google measured its own service. In 2025 it reported that the median text prompt to its Gemini apps used 0.24 watt-hours, counting the AI chips, the rest of the server, machines kept idle in reserve, and the data center’s cooling and power overhead. It also reported that the figure had fallen 33-fold in one year through better software and hardware (Elsworth et al., Google, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED] as the company’s own measurement of its own product; no outside party has audited it.

A quarter of a watt-hour would run a 9-watt LED bulb for about a minute and a half. One answer is small. A hospital’s worth of visits, every day, across thousands of hospitals, is how small numbers become a power plant.

Don’t set your laptop number beside Google’s and call a winner. They are different models doing different work, and the measurements draw their lines in different places. What the pair of numbers does show is the trade a hospital faces.

### When smaller is the better buy

A large model in a large hall is usually more capable and, per answer, often more efficient, because thousands of customers share the same machines and keep them busy. A small model in the building is less capable, but the data never leaves, the delay is short, and it keeps working when the internet is down.

For a narrow job, such as drafting a discharge summary from a fixed template or sorting faxes, a small model may be enough. For open-ended medical reasoning it probably isn’t. [PLAUSIBLE] Where exactly the line falls, in useful work per joule and per dollar, is not settled.

AnalogyThe hall is the county’s big combine: enormously productive, shared, and somewhere else when you need it. The small model is the tractor in your own shed. It does less per hour, but it’s there at 5 a.m., and nobody else has the keys.

Where it breaksA tractor does the same work every year. AI models improve fast, so a machine bought for the building can be outclassed in two years, while a cloud service upgrades itself. Owning the tractor means owning the job of replacing it.

## Rung 5. Close or far: where the computing should live

Engineers call the two choices hyperscale, meaning a few enormous data halls, and edge, meaning many small computers near the people they serve. Each wins on something real.

### Far wins on cost

Big halls spread the cost of staff, cooling, and power equipment across far more computers. They are also more efficient. PUE, power usage effectiveness, is a hall’s total energy divided by the energy that reaches the computers, so 1.0 would be perfect. In Uptime Institute’s 2023 survey, the average data center reported 1.58. Weighted by size, so that big halls count for more, the figure was 1.47 (Uptime Institute, Feb. 2024). [VERIFIED] Larger sites waste less. A closet of servers in a hospital basement will not match them. [PLAUSIBLE]

### Close wins on physics

Distance is delay, and no budget buys it back. One study cited in the standard paper on edge computing measured the round trip from 260 points around the world to the nearest Amazon data center at an average of 74 thousandths of a second, before adding the wireless hop at either end. Applications that must react as fast as a person does need the whole trip done in a few tens of thousandths (Satyanarayanan, Computer, Jan. 2017). [VERIFIED] The measurement is an older one and networks have added sites since; the physics hasn’t changed.

The same paper names four things a nearby computer does that a distant one can’t (Satyanarayanan, 2017). [VERIFIED] Each has a hospital version:

- It answers fast. A tool that watches a heart monitor or guides an ultrasound probe can’t wait on a round trip.

- It sends only the result upstream. Process the video in the building and send a one-line finding, and a thin rural connection is enough.

- It enforces privacy at the door. What never leaves the building can’t leak from someone else’s.

- It hides outages. When the fiber is cut, the local machine keeps working.

And three reasons it’s hard: scattered machines are costly to manage, a server closet is easier to walk into than a guarded data hall, and nobody builds the tools until the machines exist or the machines until the tools exist (Satyanarayanan, 2017). [VERIFIED] A 25-bed hospital with one IT employee feels the first of those hardest. [PLAUSIBLE]

### So the contract is the infrastructure

Because most hospital AI runs in a vendor’s hall today, the hospital’s protection is paper. Federal privacy law, HIPAA, lets a hospital use a cloud company to store or process patient records only if the two sign a business associate agreement that binds the company to the same rules. That holds even if the company only ever sees encrypted data and has no key (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services). [VERIFIED]

The agreement is the floor. Above it sit the questions the County Kit walks through: where recordings are kept and for how long, whether the vendor may use them to train its models, who is responsible when a note is wrong, and what the hospital gets back if it cancels.

### Where the money comes from

The federal Rural Health Transformation Program puts $50 billion into rural health over five years, $10 billion a year from 2026 through 2030. Half is split equally among approved states; the rest follows rurality and the strength of each state’s plan. First-year awards ran from $147 million to $281 million per state. Approved uses include telehealth, cybersecurity, connecting record systems, and AI scribes (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Dec. 29, 2025). [VERIFIED]

The money goes to states, not straight to hospitals. Each state decides how to pass it down. A hospital board’s first question is who in the state capital runs the program and when the next application window opens.

AnalogyThink of the county’s ambulance plan. The trauma center is far and has everything. The volunteer squad is close and has less. Nobody argues about which one to keep. The plan says which calls go where, and what the squad must be able to do alone when the road is closed.

Where it breaksAn ambulance plan is written by people who answer to the county. Where a hospital’s AI runs is usually decided by the vendor, unless the hospital writes it into the contract.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] How much useful work per joule does a small model deliver on ordinary hardware, and at what point does it become the better investment for a small hospital? Could several rural hospitals share one nearby computer the way they share a helicopter? Would a data hall in the county ever shorten the hospital’s round trip, or does its traffic leave on fiber the hospital can’t touch? Nobody has settled these. Questions for researchers, and for your vendor.

## Straight Talk

“AI does nothing for rural people.”

Wrong, but adoption is thin.

At a 25-bed hospital in Lewistown, Montana, an AI scribe cut after-hours charting so much that some physicians said they’d consider leaving without it (Becker’s Hospital Review, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] That is a recruiting tool for a hospital that can’t afford to lose one doctor.

They’re right about this part: most rural hospitals aren’t there yet, the tools make mistakes that a clinician has to catch, and a hospital on a weak connection can’t use them at all.

Ask for it in writing: if a data center deal comes to your county, tie it to broadband and AI-readiness funding for the hospital and the schools.

## What this means for your family

The question to carry out of this module is short: does this tool keep care in town?

A scribe that gives a doctor an hour back each day is one more reason for that doctor to stay. A video link to a stroke specialist can mean treatment starts before the helicopter lands. Neither works without a connection the hospital can count on and a contract somebody actually read.

If you sit on a hospital board, a county commission, or a co-op board, the kit below is the page to bring. If you’re a patient, you have one question that is always fair: is anything recording this visit, and where does the recording go?

County Kit · Module 6

Critical Access Hospital AI Readiness

A one-page checklist for a hospital board or administrator: the connection, who governs the tools, patient consent, and the vendor terms to get in writing before anything is switched on.

Open the kitOpen the kit
Download PDFDownload PDF

## Ask Earl

AI character

Is my patient data safe with one of these AI scribes?

“Depends on the paperwork and the plumbing, same as anything. Let’s trace the wire. The recording leaves the exam room and goes to somebody else’s computer. Federal rules say the hospital needs a signed agreement with that company before it handles your records. That’s verified, it’s on the Health and Human Services site. What I’d ask the front desk is three things: is that agreement signed, how long do they keep the recording, and can the company use it to train its software. I’m an AI character and no lawyer, so for anything past that, the hospital’s privacy officer is the one to call. And you can always say no to the recording.”

Ready? Five questions.

Get 4 right to pass. Retakes are fine.

Take the self-checkTake the self-check

## Sources

Every source below was opened Nov. 26, 2026.

- Rural Health Information Hub (updated Nov. 6, 2026), “Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs)”: 1,386 hospitals as of October 2026; the four eligibility conditions.

- Waghmare, N. (Aug. 3, 2026), “Innovation under pressure: 7 ways rural leaders are turning constraint into tech-driven advantage”, Becker’s Hospital Review: Central Montana Medical Center; the 8% adoption figure, for which the article names no survey.

- Rural Health Information Hub, “AI-Assisted Clinical Documentation”, Rural AI Toolkit: Patterson Health Center; reported errors; human review; consent and data retention.

Field Guide · Module 7 of 12 · July 2027

# Sun, Storage, and Flexible Load

The hottest afternoon of the year sets the size of the grid. Here’s what sun, batteries, and a customer willing to step aside can change, and what to ask for.

The decision it serves: valuing batteries, solar, and curtailment during the summer peak. About 12 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 17 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

A load that can yield on the worst days connects sooner and cheaper. A promise to yield counts only if someone can check it.

## Rung 1. The worst hour of the year

Module 1 said the grid is built for its worst hour. In most of the country that hour comes on a hot weekday in July or August, late in the afternoon. Offices are still running. People are getting home and turning the air conditioning down. Every air conditioner in three states is working at once.

That one hour sets the size of nearly everything: the power plants, the lines, the substation near your town. The equipment built for it sits partly idle the rest of the year, and everybody pays for it all year.

That’s why your co-op sends a text asking you to hold off on the dryer. Choptank Electric Cooperative in Maryland tells its members plainly that peak times are when the co-op is buying wholesale power at the highest prices, and that using less then lowers what every member pays (Choptank Electric Cooperative). [VERIFIED]

You can watch your own grid’s worst hour arrive. The federal Energy Information Administration publishes hourly demand for every grid operator in the Lower 48 states, usually within about an hour (EIA, Hourly Electric Grid Monitor). [VERIFIED] On the next hot day, look yours up and find the top of the curve.

AnalogyA church builds its parking lot for Easter Sunday. On an ordinary Tuesday the lot is nearly empty, but the paving was paid for all the same.

Where it breaksIf the lot fills on Easter, people park on the grass. If the grid runs short at its peak, something has to be switched off, on purpose and fast, or the whole system is at risk. The grid has no grass.

## Rung 2. Sun and storage move the worst hour

Solar panels make the most power around midday. People use the most power a few hours later. In between sits a gap that grid operators have a name for.

Take everything customers are using and subtract what the sun and wind are supplying. What’s left is the net load: the part that other power plants have to cover. On a sunny day the net load sags at midday, then climbs steeply toward sunset as the panels fade and the air conditioners keep going. Plotted on a chart, the line looks like a duck, so the industry calls it the duck curve (EIA, June 2023). [VERIFIED]

The hard hour moves from the hottest part of the afternoon to the hour the sun goes down.

That’s the job batteries were hired for. A grid battery fills up at midday, when solar power is plentiful and cheap, and empties in the evening. The country had 43.6 gigawatts of grid batteries at the end of 2025 and nearly 52 by mid-2026, after three years of growth averaging 70% a year (EIA, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] A gigawatt is roughly one large power plant running flat out.

Two honest limits. Most grid batteries today are built to discharge for a few hours, not a few days. [PLAUSIBLE] And a battery doesn’t make energy. It moves energy from an hour that has too much to an hour that has too little, and loses a little on the way.

## Rung 3. The other way to meet a peak: don’t

There are two ways to get through the worst hour. Build enough to cover it, or have some customers use less during it. The second is called flexible load, and when the utility asks for it, curtailment.

You already do a small version when you wait to run the dishwasher. The question for a county is whether a customer the size of a town can do it.

A 2025 Duke University study ran the numbers for the 22 largest grid areas in the country, covering about 95% of U.S. demand. It found the existing system could take on 76 gigawatts of new load if that load cut back 0.25% of the time, about 85 hours a year, and 126 gigawatts if it cut back 1% of the time, about 366 hours. Most of those hours wouldn’t need a full shutdown: on average, half the new load could keep running for 88% of the curtailment time (Duke University Nicholas Institute, as reported by Utility Dive, Feb. 2025). [VERIFIED] as a system-wide estimate.

They’re right to be skeptical about this part, and the study says so itself: it didn’t look at whether local lines and substations have room, and data centers have not historically taken part in programs like this (Utility Dive, Feb. 2025). [VERIFIED] Room on the whole system isn’t room at your substation.

Field Test: a curtailment rule for one window air conditionerA smart plug that logs energy can do on your windowsill what a utility asks of a big customer. On a hot afternoon, read the watts a window air conditioner draws. Then set the plug to switch it off for your grid’s peak hour, and put a thermometer in the room. At the end of the hour you have both sides of the bargain: watt-hours saved, and degrees gained. That trade is what a curtailment contract prices. Plug-in meters only. Not on a heat-advisory day, and not in a room where anyone is elderly, ill, or very young.

Field Test video. One room, one air conditioner, one afternoon; readings reported as measured. Plug-in meters only.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs explain why the peak matters and the two ways to meet it. The next two explain how flexibility is paid for, and how a promise to cut back gets written so that it can be enforced. They get more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them and you can read the flexibility section of a large-load contract.

## Rung 4. What flexibility is worth

### Load factor: how full the system runs

Load factor is average demand divided by peak demand. A system with a load factor of one half is, on average, half used. A customer that runs flat out around the clock, as a data hall usually does, has a load factor near one. That is good for a utility in one way: steady sales over the same wires. It is hard in another: the customer is at full draw during the worst hour, too, so it adds to the peak one for one. [PLAUSIBLE]

A flexible customer changes that arithmetic. If it can drop during the few dozen hours that set the peak, it buys energy all year without adding much to the size of the system. That is the whole idea behind the Duke estimate.

### How a battery earns its keep

A grid battery has three ways to earn money. [PLAUSIBLE] as standard industry definitions:

- Arbitrage. Buy power when it’s cheap, sell when it’s dear. This is the duck curve turned into income.

- Capacity. Get paid simply for being available at the peak, the way a volunteer fire department is funded to be ready.

- Fast response. The grid has to hold its frequency steady second by second. A battery can react in a fraction of a second, faster than any turbine.

A battery at a data hall can do a fourth thing: carry the hall through its own curtailment. The hall keeps computing; the grid sees the load drop. That is why “on-site batteries” belongs on a county’s list of terms.

### What the big customers have actually signed

This is no longer theory. Google reported in March 2026 that it had put 1 gigawatt of data center demand response into long-term contracts with five utilities: Indiana Michigan Power, the Tennessee Valley Authority, Entergy Arkansas, Minnesota Power, and DTE Energy. Under those contracts it can pause or shift part of its machine-learning work when the grid is strained (Google, March 2026). [VERIFIED] as the company’s own announcement.

The same announcement concedes the limit: there are limits to how flexible a given data center can be, and the capability will only be available at certain locations. It doesn’t say how many hours a year the contracts cover (Google, March 2026). [VERIFIED] A county should ask for that number.

AnalogyAn irrigation district in a dry year doesn’t build a new reservoir for August. Farmers with junior rights agree ahead of time to shut their gates when the river drops, and they pay less for water because of it.

Where it breaksA ditch rider can see a closed gate from the road. Nobody can see a data hall using less power. It takes a meter, a record, and someone with the right to read both.

## Rung 5. A promise you can check

### What one state wrote into law

Texas put flexibility into statute in 2025. Senate Bill 6 covers new customers that connect at transmission voltage, the high-voltage level where big data centers plug in. Before one connects, it must install equipment that lets its load be cut off during a firm load shed, the grid’s last-resort emergency step of switching customers off in rotation. A large customer with backup generators can be ordered, on reasonable notice, to run them or cut its load. And the grid operator must set up a program that pays large customers of 75 megawatts or more, chosen by competitive bid, to reduce demand with at least 24 hours’ notice (Texas Senate Research Center, bill analysis of S.B. 6, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED]

Notice the three different things in that one law. A switch someone else controls. An order to run generators. A paid, bid-for reduction. They are not equally good for the neighbors.

### The generator question

The cheapest way for a data hall to “curtail” is to start its backup diesel generators and take itself off the grid. The grid sees less demand. The people downwind get the exhaust, on the hottest days of the year.

Federal air rules put a ceiling on that. Emergency engines can run without an hourly limit in a true emergency, but only 100 hours a year for other purposes, and within that, up to 50 hours a year for demand response under set conditions, including being dispatched by the local grid operator and keeping records (U.S. Environmental Protection Agency guidance, as reported by the American Public Power Association, May 2025). [VERIFIED] That guidance is a letter, not a binding rule, and the agency has said it is weighing further changes.

So a county has a fair question that the federal rule doesn’t settle: when this customer says it will be flexible, will it use less power, run a battery, or burn diesel? The answer can be written into a permit or an agreement. [PLAUSIBLE]

### Four things that make a promise checkable

Reasoned from the examples above, a flexibility term is enforceable when it names four things. [PLAUSIBLE]

- The amount and the hours. How many megawatts, for how many hours a year, on how much notice.

- The method. Reduced computing, on-site batteries, or generators, and a cap on generator hours.

- The meter. Who measures the drop, against what baseline, and who can see the record.

- The consequence. What the customer pays if it doesn’t deliver. A discount for flexibility with no penalty for failing is a discount.

### Why this is the county’s leverage

Module 1 showed that connecting to the grid can take years. A customer that will yield at the peak needs less new equipment built for it, so it can often be connected sooner. [PLAUSIBLE] Speed is worth a great deal to a developer. That is the trade a co-op board or a county can offer: a faster yes, in exchange for flexibility that is written down, metered, and enforced.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] How much of a modern AI data hall’s work can really wait an hour, or four? Will flexible contracts hold when a customer’s own deadline collides with a heat wave? If every large load on a system promises to cut back in the same emergency, has the system counted the same megawatt twice? Nobody has settled these. Questions for researchers, and for your utility.

## Straight Talk

“Data centers can never cut back.”

Overstated. Some can, some of the time, and the contract has to say how much.

One operator has signed 1 gigawatt of demand response into contracts with five utilities (Google, March 2026). [VERIFIED] as the company’s own announcement. Texas law now requires new customers on the high-voltage grid to be able to be cut off in an emergency (S.B. 6, 2025). [VERIFIED]

They’re right about this part: the same operator says flexibility has limits and is available only at some sites, and a hall can meet its promise by burning diesel instead of using less.

Ask for it in writing: megawatts, hours per year, the method, who meters it, and what it costs them to break the promise.

## What this means for your family

The peak is where a new customer either raises everybody’s costs or doesn’t. If a big load adds to the worst hour, the system has to grow to carry it, and Module 2 showed who can end up paying for that growth. If the load steps aside during that hour, the same wires serve more sales, and that can hold rates down. [PLAUSIBLE]

It also decides what the air is like on the hottest days. A row of diesel generators running through a heat wave is a different neighbor from a battery.

If you’re a co-op member, the question for the annual meeting is short: for our largest customers, what can we ask them to do at the peak, and how do we know they did it?

Open the kitOpen the kit
Download PDFDownload PDF

## Ask Earl

AI character

Why does my co-op beg me to cut back at 5 p.m.?

“Because that’s the hour the whole system is sized for, and the hour the co-op pays the most for the power it buys. Everything from the plant to the pot on your pole has to be big enough for that one stretch of a hot afternoon. If the members shave a little off the top, the co-op’s power bill comes down, and since you own the place, so does yours. Nobody’s asking you to sit in the heat. Run the dryer after supper and nudge the thermostat up a couple of degrees. And if you’ve got somebody at home who doesn’t do well in the heat, leave the air on. That one’s not worth the savings.”

Ready? Five questions.

Get 4 right to pass. Retakes are fine.

Take the self-checkTake the self-check

Every source below was opened Nov. 26, 2026.

- Choptank Electric Cooperative, “Beat the Peak FAQ”: peak times and wholesale power cost.

- U.S. Energy Information Administration, “About the EIA-930 data” (Hourly Electric Grid Monitor): hourly demand and generation by grid operator.

- U.S. Energy Information Administration (June 21, 2023), “As solar capacity grows, duck curves are getting deeper in California”: net load and the duck curve.

- U.S. Energy Information Administration (Aug. 7, 2026), “Battery storage capacity averaged 70% growth over the last three years”: 43.6 GW at end of 2025; nearly 52 GW by mid-2026.

- Howland, E. (Feb. 11, 2025), “US grid has headroom for flexible loads, Duke report finds”, Utility Dive, reporting Norris et al., Rethinking Load Growth, Duke University Nicholas Institute: 76 GW and 126 GW; hours of curtailment; limits of the study.

### Go deeper (rungs 4 and 5), opened Nov. 26, 2026

- Terrell, M. (March 19, 2026), “A new milestone for smart, affordable electricity growth”, Google: 1 GW of demand response; five utilities; stated limits.

- Texas Senate Research Center (Aug. 5, 2025), bill analysis, S.B. 6 (enrolled): 75-megawatt threshold; curtailment equipment; backup generation; competitively procured demand reduction with 24-hour notice.

- American Public Power Association (May 19, 2025), “EPA clarifies backup generator use for grid stability”: 100-hour and 50-hour limits and conditions for emergency engines.

Field Guide · Module 8 of 12 · August 2027

# The Jobs Question

Every data center proposal arrives with a jobs number. Here’s how to take it apart, what the research says, and how to make sure some of those jobs go to people who live here.

The decision it serves: judging job promises and building a training pipeline. About 12 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 17 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Construction jobs are many and temporary; operating jobs are few and good. Plan for both, and put the hiring in writing.

## Rung 1. Two kinds of jobs

When a data center is proposed, the first number in the room is usually a jobs number. Before you weigh it, split it in two.

Construction jobs build the place: site crews, ironworkers, concrete, electricians, pipefitters. There are a lot of them, and they end when the building is finished. Many of the workers travel from job to job and go home when it’s done.

Operating jobs run the place afterward: technicians who keep the power and cooling going, people who swap failed parts, security, and managers. There are far fewer of these, and they tend to pay well and last.

Both kinds are real. They are not the same kind of promise. A job that lasts eighteen months and a job that lasts twenty years shouldn’t be added together into one number, and when they are, it’s fair to ask for them back apart.

AnalogyBuilding a grain elevator takes a big crew for a season. Running it takes a manager and a few hands. Nobody in town confuses the two, and nobody thinks the elevator is worthless because it only employs five.

Where it breaksThe elevator buys what the county grows, so its money circulates here. A data hall’s customers and most of its suppliers are somewhere else. Its value to the county has to be arranged on purpose: taxes, training, fiber, and the terms in this module.

## Rung 2. What the studies find

Two research teams looked at what happened in counties that got data centers, and they agree on more than they disagree.

Georgia Tech researchers matched individual facilities to county economic records. They found that rural facilities typically employ few permanent workers, often fewer than 100, and that many specialized services are brought in from outside the county. Counties in metro areas saw gains in jobs and new businesses. Counties outside metro areas saw few measurable gains beyond a small drop in unemployment. Across all host counties, employment rose about 0.9% and wages about 1.1% in the first three years (Yue and Zeng, Georgia Tech, as reported by Futurity, July 2026). [VERIFIED]

Brookings researchers compared about 1,500 built facilities with 52 that were announced and then canceled. That comparison matters, because counties that attract data centers were already growing faster than their neighbors. They found large percentage gains in two narrow industries over the first ten years, data processing up 56% and telecommunications up 43%, which works out to roughly 100 to 200 jobs in a typical county. Wages didn’t change. Home prices rose 2% to 5% (Bahar and Wright, Brookings Institution, updated Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] Brookings discloses that it receives unrestricted donations from Amazon, Google, Meta, and Microsoft, and says the findings are the authors’ own.

So the honest summary is this. The jobs are real, they number in the dozens to low hundreds, and in a rural county they don’t automatically go to people who live there.

Field Test: find the dead battery the way a technician wouldMuch of an operating job is finding the one bad part in a long chain. Put eight AA batteries in an eight-cell holder, with one used-up battery hidden among them. Checking them one at a time takes up to eight readings. A technician uses the half-split method instead: measure across the first four with a $20 multimeter. The half that reads low holds the bad one. Split that half, then split again. Three readings, every time. Small batteries only. A multimeter never goes near a wall outlet, a panel, or a car battery in this test.

Field Test video. Eight AA batteries, one multimeter, one afternoon; readings reported as measured. Handheld meters only.

## Rung 3. Who gets the good jobs

The operating jobs go to people with a trade: electricians, heating and cooling mechanics, controls technicians. Whether those people come from your county depends on whether your county trains them.

Take electricians. The typical way in is a high school diploma and a four- or five-year apprenticeship, which is a paid job with classroom instruction alongside it. Median pay was $63,190 a year in May 2025. The Bureau of Labor Statistics expects the trade to grow 9% from 2025 to 2035, with about 72,700 openings a year (U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] That is a national figure for all electricians, not a data center wage.

Veterans have a head start and a benefit. Someone who qualifies for the GI Bill can use it during an apprenticeship or on-the-job training, receiving a monthly payment for living expenses, and under the Post-9/11 GI Bill, money for books and supplies (U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs). [VERIFIED]

And the industry needs the help. In Uptime Institute’s 2026 survey of data center operators, more than half said they had difficulty finding qualified candidates for open positions (Uptime Institute, July 2026). [VERIFIED]

That shortage is the county’s leverage. An operator that can’t find technicians has its own reason to pay for a training program at the community college. The time to ask is before the permit, and the place to put the answer is the agreement.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs explain which jobs are real and who gets them. The next two explain how a jobs number is built, and how to write a hiring commitment that holds up. They get more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them and you can question an economic impact study at a public hearing.

## Rung 4. How a jobs number is built

The figure in a press release usually comes from an economic impact study paid for by the developer or an economic development agency. These studies follow standard methods, and the methods leave room. Four questions take most of the air out of a large number. [PLAUSIBLE] as a description of standard practice.

### Is it jobs, or job-years?

A job-year is one person working for one year. A project that employs 500 people for two years of construction can be described as 1,000 job-years, and somewhere between the study and the headline the word “years” tends to fall off.

### Direct, indirect, or induced?

Direct jobs are on the project’s own payroll. Indirect jobs are at its suppliers. Induced jobs come from workers spending their pay at the diner and the hardware store. The second and third are estimated with a multiplier, and a multiplier built for a metro area overstates what happens in a county where the suppliers and the big-box stores are somewhere else. The Georgia Tech finding that specialized services come from outside the county is that same leak, measured. [PLAUSIBLE]

### Compared with what?

A county that lands a data center was often growing already. Comparing it with a county that never had a chance credits the data center with growth that was coming anyway. That is why the Brookings team compared built projects with canceled ones, and why they warn that a simple before-and-after comparison overstates the job effect (Bahar and Wright, 2026). [VERIFIED]

### What did each job cost?

Divide the tax breaks by the permanent jobs. The Brookings study found state incentives worth about 2% of construction investment in counties with the largest, company-owned facilities, and about 62% in counties whose facilities lease space to others (Bahar and Wright, 2026). [VERIFIED] The same word, “incentive,” covers a rounding error and most of the building.

None of this means the study is dishonest. It means the headline is the top of a range, and the county is entitled to see the range.

AnalogyA seed dealer’s yield number comes from a test plot: good ground, perfect rain, every input on time. It’s a real number. It isn’t your field.

Where it breaksYou can plant a strip and check the dealer’s number in one season. A county can’t run the project twice. The only check it gets is the one it writes into the agreement: report the hires every year, and pay something back if they fall short.

## Rung 5. Writing a workforce clause that holds

### What a clause needs

A hiring promise in a slide deck binds no one. A term in a signed agreement can. Reasoned from how these agreements are built, a workforce clause holds when it does five things. [PLAUSIBLE]

- Defines “local.” Residents of the county, or of named neighboring counties, on the day they’re hired. Without a definition, a worker who rents a room for the job counts.

- Sets separate targets for construction and for operations, as a share of hours worked or of positions filled.

- Funds the pipeline early. Money and equipment for the community college or the high school career center, starting before construction, so graduates exist when hiring begins.

- Requires apprentices. A share of construction hours worked by registered apprentices, so the project leaves trained people behind.

- Reports and enforces. A yearly public report of hires by home county, and a consequence, such as a reduced abatement, if a target is missed.

### What one county’s offer looked like

In September 2026 a developer offered Frederick County, Maryland, $110 million in community benefits for a 2,100-acre data center campus. The package included $14.5 million for a workforce training center and career and technical education. It did not include a local hiring requirement. In return the developer asked the county not to change zoning in ways that could hurt the project for eight years. After hundreds of public comments, the county executive rejected the agreement two weeks later and extended a moratorium on data center applications to July 1, 2027 (WYPR, Sept. 15, 2026; Maryland Association of Counties, Sept. 2, 2026). [VERIFIED]

Two lessons sit in that story, whichever side you’d have taken. Money for a training center is not a commitment to hire the people it trains. And every benefit has a price on the other side of the page; read what the county is asked to give up.

### Can a county require local hiring?

It depends on the state, and on whether the term is a condition of a permit or part of a negotiated agreement tied to an incentive. A county can usually attach conditions to money it’s giving up; what it can impose outright is narrower. [PLAUSIBLE] This is a question for the county attorney before the first meeting, not after the last one.

### Tie it to the abatement

Most of a county’s leverage is the tax break. If the project is getting one, the hiring targets belong in the same document, on the same schedule, with the break shrinking if the targets are missed. The Straight Talk library has both ends of what abatements can do: Loudoun County, Virginia, reports the industry generates nearly half its property tax revenue, while El Paso granted an 80% abatement over 35 years. [VERIFIED]

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Does a training program paid for by one operator keep its graduates in the county, or train them for jobs two states away? As halls automate more of their own maintenance, do the operating jobs shrink further? Could a rural county do better by training its people for the regional construction circuit than by counting on one building? Nobody has settled these. Questions for researchers, and for your community college.

## Straight Talk

“It’ll bring hundreds of jobs.”

Wrong for permanent jobs.

Rural facilities often employ fewer than 100 permanent workers, and specialized services come from outside the county (Georgia Tech, as reported by Futurity, July 2026). [VERIFIED] Construction jobs are real but temporary.

They’re right about this part: the permanent jobs that do exist are skilled, and operators say they can’t find enough people to fill them.

Ask for it in writing: local-hire targets, apprenticeships, and a community college partnership, in the agreement itself.

## What this means for your family

The question to carry is whether a kid from your county can get one of these jobs without leaving, and whether someone mid-career can retrain into one.

That depends less on the data center than on what is in place around it: a program at the community college, an apprenticeship with open seats, a counselor who knows the path exists. A veteran with a logistics or electrical specialty is closer to these jobs than most, and has a benefit that pays during the training.

A trade learned on one project doesn’t expire when the project does. Electricians, mechanics, and controls technicians are needed at the hospital, the co-op, the water plant, and the school. Training is the one benefit that stays if the building doesn’t.

Field Guide · Module 9 of 12 · September 2027

# AI on the Farm

Precision farming tools are computers making decisions about your ground. Here’s where those computers sit, what they need from your signal, and what to read before you sign.

The decision it serves: choosing precision-ag tools, and where the computing should happen. About 12 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 16 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Some decisions can’t wait for a round trip to the cloud. Before you buy, ask what the tool does with no signal, and who ends up holding your data.

## Rung 1. A decision that can’t wait

Precision agriculture means treating each part of a field according to what that part needs, instead of treating the whole field the same. A planter that changes its seeding rate as the soil changes. A sprayer that sprays the weed and skips the bare ground. A yield monitor that maps where the crop came in heavy and where it didn’t.

Every one of those is a computer making a decision. The question this module asks is where that computer sits.

Some decisions are slow. Which hybrid to plant next spring can be worked out over the winter, on a big computer a thousand miles away. Call that the cloud: somebody else’s data hall, reached over the internet.

Some decisions are fast. A sprayer rolling across a field has a fraction of a second to decide whether the green thing under its boom is a weed. That decision has to be made on the machine. Engineers call a computer that sits where the work happens the edge.

AnalogyYou’d mail a soil sample to the lab and wait a week for the report. You wouldn’t mail the lab a question about whether to swerve around a rock.

Where it breaksThe lab and the tractor seat aren’t really separate. The fast decision on the machine is made by a model that was built, slowly, in a data hall, from other people’s fields, and the machine sends its own records back afterward. Edge and cloud are two ends of one system.

## Rung 2. What the tools do, and who is using them

Start with a tool that works. One manufacturer’s camera-guided sprayer carries cameras and processors on the boom, identifies weeds as it passes, and opens individual nozzles only over them. The company reports its customers ran it on more than 5 million acres in 2025 and cut their use of non-residual herbicide by nearly 50% on average, at speeds up to 15 miles an hour (Deere & Co. news release, Nov. 2025). [VERIFIED] as the company’s own report of its own product; no independent audit is cited.

Now the wider picture, which is thinner. In a 2025 federal survey, 22% of U.S. farms used precision agriculture practices, down from 27% in 2023 (USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED] The survey counts farms of every size.

Congress’s auditors looked at why. The benefits they list are real: the same yield with less fertilizer, herbicide, fuel, and water, and less runoff. The obstacles are real too: equipment that costs more than a smaller farm can justify, brands that won’t work together, and farmers who don’t trust what happens to their data (U.S. Government Accountability Office, Jan. 2024). [VERIFIED]

They’re right to be cautious. A tool that pays on 5,000 acres may never pay on 300, and a subscription is a cost every year whether or not the crop comes in.

## Rung 3. Coverage on the map, signal in the field

Whatever a tool decides on the machine, it still needs a connection sooner or later: to download its maps, upload its records, and get its updates.

Here is how farms connect. In the same 2025 survey, 85% of U.S. farms had internet access. Counting every type a farm uses, 74% connected through a cellular data plan, 55% through a wired broadband line, and 24% by satellite (USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED]

Two cautions about numbers like that. First, they describe the farm, which usually means the house and the shop. They say nothing about the far corner of the back forty. Second, the federal broadband maps count where a provider says service is available; the map can show coverage where a tractor cab shows no bars. [PLAUSIBLE] The only reading that counts is one you take yourself, in the place the machine will be working.

Two things to measure. Speed is how much data moves per second. Latency is the delay for one round trip, in thousandths of a second, or milliseconds. A tool that uploads a yield map overnight cares about speed. A tool that expects an answer back while the machine is moving cares about latency.

Field Test: latency at the house, the field edge, and the far fencePut a free speed-test app on your phone. Stand at the house and run it three times; write down download, upload, and latency. Do the same at the edge of a field, and again at the fence farthest from the road. Note the carrier and the number of bars each time. Now you have a coverage map nobody can argue with, made by the person who farms the ground. Phone-app readings are [PLAUSIBLE], not lab measurements, and they change with weather and time of day. Phone only. Walk or drive the field as you normally would, and never run the test from a moving tractor seat.

Field Test video. One phone, one carrier, one afternoon; readings reported as measured. Phone-app readings are PLAUSIBLE.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs explain what these tools do and what they need. The next two explain the arithmetic that forces some computing onto the machine, and the question of who holds the data it produces. They get more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them and you can read a technology contract before you sign it.

## Rung 4. The arithmetic of a round trip

### How far does the machine move while it waits?

Take the sprayer at 15 miles an hour. That is 22 feet every second.

Now suppose it had to ask a distant data hall whether to spray. One widely cited measurement put the average round trip from 260 points around the world to the nearest large cloud site at 74 milliseconds, before adding the wireless hop at either end (Satyanarayanan, Computer, Jan. 2017). [VERIFIED] The measurement is an older one, and a rural cellular link adds delay of its own.

In 74 milliseconds the sprayer travels 22 feet per second × 0.074 seconds, which is about 1.6 feet. [VERIFIED] as arithmetic on the two figures above. The weed is behind the nozzle before the answer arrives. And that is the best case, with a signal. With no signal there is no answer at all.

So the decision is made on the boom. Not because the cloud is weak, but because distance is delay, and a moving machine can’t spend it.

### Send the answer, not the pictures

The same paper names a second reason to compute at the edge: a nearby computer can boil a flood of raw data down to a small result and send only that (Satyanarayanan, 2017). [VERIFIED] By the company’s account, that sprayer’s cameras scan more than 2,500 square feet of ground every second. No rural connection carries that much video. What the machine can send, later, from the shop, is the summary: where it sprayed and how much. [PLAUSIBLE]

### A latency budget

Engineers sort jobs by how long they can wait. You can do the same with any tool you’re offered. [PLAUSIBLE] as a way of sorting, not a standard.

- Thousandths of a second. Steering, spraying, anything tied to a moving machine. This has to run on the machine.

- Seconds to minutes. A grain cart finding the combine, an alert that a pivot has stopped. A local link is enough; the cloud is optional.

- Hours to seasons. Yield analysis, seed selection, marketing. The cloud is fine, and a slow connection overnight will do.

A tool that puts a first-row job on a third-row connection will fail in the field, and the field is where you’ll find out.

AnalogyA combine operator and a grain cart driver work by hand signals and a glance, because that’s fast enough. The elevator’s price comes by phone, because that can wait a minute. Nobody runs the hand signals through the elevator.

Where it breaksTwo people in a field can always see each other. A machine at the edge only knows what it was taught before it left the shop. If the weeds changed this year, it finds out when someone updates it, and that update comes down the same thin connection.

## Rung 5. Who holds the harvest of data

### Ownership is a principle; control is a contract

Every pass across a field now produces a record: what was planted, sprayed, and harvested, where, and when. Whose is it?

The farm groups and equipment companies that wrote the industry’s Privacy and Security Principles for Farm Data put it plainly: farmers own the information generated on their operations. But that is a principle the industry agreed to, not a rule of law. The same extension guide that explains it says what actually governs is the written agreement between the farmer and the technology company, and that ownership gets murky when a landlord, a tenant, and a custom applicator all have a hand in the same field (Ohio State University Extension, 2018). [VERIFIED]

That guide lists what to look for in the agreement: who may collect and see the data, why, whether you can opt out of pieces, whether you can take your data to another company, whether it can be sold or shared, how long it’s kept, what happens when you cancel, and whether the company is barred from using it to trade in commodity markets (Ohio State University Extension, 2018). [VERIFIED] The County Kit turns that list into a one-page sheet.

### Why this matters more with AI

An AI model is built from data. The sprayer that knows a weed from a soybean learned it from pictures of many farmers’ fields. That is a fair trade if the terms say so. Congress’s auditors found that concerns over data sharing and ownership are themselves an obstacle to using AI in agriculture: farmers worry about losing a competitive edge, about security, and about drawing regulatory attention (U.S. Government Accountability Office, Jan. 2024). [VERIFIED]

The same report names the other lock: without common standards, one brand’s equipment and records may not work with another’s (GAO, Jan. 2024). [VERIFIED] Data you can’t move is data you don’t control, whatever the contract calls it. [PLAUSIBLE]

### What a county has to do with it

Module 6 made the case that a hospital’s AI is only as good as its connection. A farm’s is the same. When fiber or a tower comes to a county as part of a larger project, where it runs decides which farms can use these tools. [PLAUSIBLE] A route that passes the school, the clinic, and the farm-to-market roads is worth asking for by name.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Could farmers pool their data in a cooperative they own, the way they pooled grain, and license it on their own terms? Would a small shared computer at the co-op or the elevator serve a neighborhood of farms better than a signal to a distant hall? Does precision equipment ever pay on a small farm if it’s shared or hired by the acre? Nobody has settled these. Questions for researchers, and for your extension office.

## Straight Talk

“My farm data is mine automatically.”

It depends on what you signed.

The industry’s own principles say farmers own the information generated on their operations. Those are principles, not law; the written agreement decides who can collect, use, share, and keep the data (Ohio State University Extension, 2018). [VERIFIED]

They’re right about this part: farmers’ distrust of how their data is handled is well founded enough that federal auditors list it as a barrier to adoption (GAO, Jan. 2024). [VERIFIED]

Ask for it in writing: who can see the data, whether it can be sold, whether you can take it with you, and what gets deleted when you leave.

## What this means for your family

For a farm family the question is whether a tool earns more than it costs, on your acres, with your signal. Three things to settle before the check is written: what it does with no connection, what it costs every year after the first, and what happens to your records if you switch brands or quit.

For the kid in 4-H or FFA, this is a career that doesn’t require leaving. Somebody has to install, calibrate, and repair these machines, and that somebody needs to know both a wiring diagram and a field.

And for the county, farm connectivity is infrastructure, the same as a bridge that can carry a loaded grain truck. It belongs on the list when anyone is negotiating over fiber.

Farm Data and Connectivity

A one-page checklist to fill in before you buy or subscribe: your own signal readings, what the tool does offline, and the data terms to find in the agreement.

Open the kitOpen the kit
Download PDFDownload PDF

## Ask Earl

AI character

The map says I’ve got coverage. Why is there no signal in my back forty?

“Because the map and the field are two different things. The map shows where a company says it can serve. It doesn’t know about your creek bottom or the hill between you and the tower. So don’t argue with the map, measure the field. Take your phone to the house, the field edge, and the far fence, run a speed test three times at each, and write down what you get. That’s a plausible reading, not a lab number, but it’s yours, and it’s from the spot that matters. Then before you buy anything that needs a signal, ask the dealer one thing: what does it do out there when it’s got none? Ask for that in writing. And do your testing on foot. Never fool with a phone from a moving tractor seat.”

Ready? Five questions.
