Field Guide · Module 10 of 12 · October 2027

# Making the Deal

A developer’s promise and a county’s contract are two different things. Here’s how to tell them apart before anyone signs.

The decision it serves: negotiating a community benefit agreement. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 27 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

A promise is worth what its enforcement clause says.

## Rung 1. A promise and a contract are different things

When a big project comes to a county, the promises come first: jobs, tax money, a new park, help for the school. Some arrive in a press release. Some are said out loud at a meeting. A few end up in a signed contract.

Only the last kind can be collected. A community benefit agreement is that contract: a legally binding agreement between a developer and a local government, local community groups, or both. The developer commits to specific benefits. In return, the community agrees to support the project, or at least not to fight it (Columbia Law School, Sabin Center, May 2026). [VERIFIED]

Ask four questions of any promise, and you’ll know which kind it is:

- Who signed it? A name on a contract can be held to it. A quote in a newspaper can’t.

- When is it paid? “Over the life of the project” is not a date.

- What backs it? If the company is sold or goes broke, is the money already set aside?

- Who checks? Someone has to measure whether the promise was kept, and say so in public.

The rest of this module is those four questions, one at a time.

AnalogyA man selling a used truck says, “She runs great.” A dealer hands you a written warranty that says what gets fixed, for how long, and who pays. Both are promises. Only one of them is worth anything the day the transmission goes.

Where it breaksYou can look under a truck’s hood today. A data center deal runs twenty years or more, and you can’t inspect year twelve. So the paper has to say now what happens then.

## Rung 2. The four clauses that make a deal real

There aren’t many of these agreements to study yet. In August 2026 the Federation of American Scientists went looking and could find only eight signed benefit agreements for data centers in the whole country. Only one, in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, was posted where the public could read it; the others took news searches and public-records requests to find (Federation of American Scientists, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] So the examples below are a short list, and Lancaster shows up often because it’s the one everybody can read.

### 1. Say it in numbers

A term can only be enforced if a judge can tell whether it was met. Lancaster’s agreement caps water at 20,000 gallons a day for each campus (City of Lancaster). [VERIFIED] That’s a number. A meter can check it.

The same agreement’s hiring plan asks only for “good faith efforts,” with no minimum number or share of local hires, and other terms lean on phrases like “where feasible.” A Columbia Law School review called those terms hard to enforce (Sabin Center, May 2026). [VERIFIED] The critics who say much of this language is soft are right about that part.

### 2. Put dates on the money

A payment schedule says how much is due and what triggers it. Lancaster’s developers owe $20 million, split between two $10 million funds. Each fund gets $2.5 million when a building’s construction financing closes and $2.5 million within 30 days of that building starting to operate (City of Lancaster). [VERIFIED] In Festus, Missouri, the schedule is by year: $3 million a year for years one through five, then $5 million a year for years six through ten (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

The best triggers are things the developer needs anyway: a permit, a financing closing, the day the power turns on. A payment tied to “profitability” may never come due. [PLAUSIBLE]

### 3. Set the money aside

Security is money or property pledged ahead of time, so the county doesn’t have to chase a company that has left. The common forms:

- A letter of credit: a bank’s written promise to pay the county if the developer doesn’t.

- Escrow: cash held by a neutral third party until a condition is met.

- A lien: a legal claim on the property itself.

- A bond: an insurer’s guarantee, often used to pay for removing a facility at the end of its life.

Lancaster holds a $10 million letter of credit tied to the developers’ clean-energy commitment, and the city says it can draw on financial security if a payment is missed (Sabin Center, May 2026; City of Lancaster). [VERIFIED] Marysville, Ohio, uses a lien that lets it recover up to 100% of taxes for the year a facility shuts down plus the two years before, if it stays closed more than a year (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

Most places skip this. In a review of 42 local data center actions, bonds for decommissioning or financial assurance appeared in four (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

### 4. Make someone report, in public

A promise nobody measures is a promise nobody can enforce. Lancaster’s developers must report on clean-energy use at a public city council meeting every April. St. Louis requires a yearly noise report from a third party. El Paso’s agreement allows one escorted inspection a year (City of Lancaster; Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

A report from the company about itself is a start. A reading taken by somebody the company doesn’t pay is better. Rung 3 explains why.

### And the line that ties them together

The enforcement clause says what the county can do when a term is broken. It usually gives the developer written notice and a cure period, a set number of days to fix the problem; 30 to 60 days is typical in the agreements reviewed (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED] After that, Lancaster can ask a court to order compliance, and its strongest remedy is making the data center stop operating (City of Lancaster). [VERIFIED] St. Louis wrote in liquidated damages, a dollar amount fixed ahead of time, for missed hiring targets (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

Read that clause first. Everything else in the agreement is worth what it says.

## Rung 3. Copies are not independence

Data centers are built by people who think hard about failure. Their vocabulary is worth borrowing, because it applies to contracts as well as to cooling.

Engineers count backup equipment against what’s needed. N is exactly enough. N+1 is one spare. 2N is two complete systems, each able to carry the whole load. The Uptime Institute’s four Tiers, which you’ll hear quoted in sales pitches, describe how much of this a building has: Tier I is basic capacity, Tier II adds redundant parts, Tier III can be maintained without a shutdown, and Tier IV is built to keep running through a failure (Uptime Institute, April 2021). [VERIFIED]

Here’s the arithmetic. Take two parts that each work 99% of the time.

- Wire them in a chain, so both must work: 0.99 × 0.99 = 98.01%. That’s about 174 hours down in a year.

- Wire them side by side, so either one will do: the system fails only when both fail at once, 1% of 1% of the time. That’s 99.99%, under one hour down in a year.

Side by side looks almost perfect. But the math has a condition hidden in it: the two parts must fail independently. If one storm, one bad software update, or one shared power feed takes out both, you never had two. You had one, twice. Engineers call that a common-mode failure, and it’s why 2N means two separate paths, not two copies on the same path. [PLAUSIBLE]

Field Test: unplug the meshIf your house has mesh Wi-Fi, you own a small lesson in this. Run a speed test on your phone and write down the number. Unplug one of the far points from the wall and test again: you’re still online, maybe slower. That’s a spare doing its job. Plug it back in, wait for it to reconnect, then unplug the point that’s wired to your modem. Now every point in the house is still lit and still broadcasting, and none of them can reach the internet. Three points, one path out. Speed-test apps are rough tools, so your numbers are estimates. [PLAUSIBLE] Unplug at the wall only. Never open the equipment.

Field Test video. One house, one mesh system, one day; readings reported as measured. Plug-in meters only.

Now read a deal the same way. Suppose a developer promises a park, a school payment, and a noise limit, and all three are owed by one company set up for this one project. That’s three promises on one path. If that company is sold or runs out of money, all three fail together.

Independence in a contract looks like this:

- The money is held by a bank, not by the company that owes it.

- The obligations are recorded against the land, so they bind whoever owns it next.

- The measurements come from a third party, not from the company being measured.

- The county has a remedy it can use by itself, without the developer’s cooperation.

One more thing about those Tier numbers. People often attach an uptime percentage to each Tier. The Uptime Institute took every “expected downtime per year” figure out of its standard in 2009, because how a building is run matters as much as how it’s built (Uptime Institute, April 2021). [VERIFIED] A backup makes failure less likely. It doesn’t make it impossible, and a contract shouldn’t assume it does.

AnalogyN+1 is a spare tire. 2N is a second truck. The spare handles the most likely trouble cheaply. The second truck handles nearly everything, at twice the price.

Where it breaksTires go flat one at a time. Real failures often come together, like two trucks parked under the same tree in the same storm. A second truck only helps if it’s parked somewhere else.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs give you the test for any promise. The next two follow the money and the power through the contract: what the county gives up in exchange, who pays if the customer leaves, and how a promise to use the grid gently gets written so it can be checked. They’re more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them before you sit down across the table.

## Rung 4. What the county gives, and who holds the risk

A contract needs something of value moving in both directions. Lawyers call it consideration. The developer’s side is the benefits. The community’s side is usually support, or a promise not to oppose the project (Sabin Center, May 2026). [VERIFIED] Often the local government adds something far larger: a tax break, or a promise not to change the rules.

### Price what you’re giving

A tax abatement is a discount on taxes the project would otherwise owe. They can be very large. El Paso granted an 80% property tax abatement over 35 years (Brookings Institution, Jan. 2026). [VERIFIED] Cedar Rapids, Iowa, agreed to a 70% rebate over 20 years, estimated at $529 million out of as much as $1 billion in expected property taxes (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

So the honest number for any deal is the net: benefits promised, minus taxes forgiven, for each taxing district. A deal can still be worth doing after that subtraction. But a county that only hears the first number hasn’t heard the deal. Some agreements tie the discount to results with a clawback, a clause that takes the benefit back if a target is missed. El Paso’s abatement shrinks if the project doesn’t reach 50 jobs or $800 million in investment (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

### A deal that didn’t close: Frederick County

On September 1, 2026, Frederick County, Maryland, announced a proposed agreement with the developer of a 2,100-acre data center campus: more than $110 million in benefits, including $30 million to renovate an elementary school, $14.5 million for a workforce training center, and $10.5 million to preserve farmland. The developer also offered to build nearly 20% less and cut drinking-water use by 80% (Maryland Association of Counties, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

In return, the county would agree not to make zoning changes that hurt the project for eight years. Residents had ten days to comment. Hundreds did. Many said the county was giving up too much local authority, and that the benefits weren’t defined clearly enough. On September 14 the county executive rejected the agreement and extended the county’s pause on data center applications to July 1, 2027 (WYPR, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED]

Read the draft against Rung 2 and you can see both sides. It had real strengths: dated payments, obligations that bound future owners and ran with the land, and a requirement that the county approve any transfer. But in the unsigned draft that was made public, we found no bond, escrow, or letter of credit backing the benefit payments themselves. [PLAUSIBLE] That grade is ours: it’s our reading of one draft, not a legal opinion.

Frederick isn’t a story about a good deal or a bad one. It’s a reminder that the largest number in the press release is one term out of many, and that ten days is not long to read the rest.

### The capital chain: who pays if the customer leaves

A benefit agreement covers what the developer owes the county. It doesn’t cover what the developer owes the power system. That’s the job of a large-load tariff, the utility rule from Module 2 that makes a big customer carry the cost of the equipment built for it. Ohio’s regulators, for example, require large new data centers to pay for at least 85% of the power they sign up for, whether they use it or not, for up to 12 years (Brookings Institution, Jan. 2026). [VERIFIED] As of May 2026, 23 states had approved at least one such tariff (Columbia Sabin Center, in the Straight Talk library). [VERIFIED]

The same goes for zoning. A benefit agreement can’t patch a hole in the ordinance; the two have to back each other up (Federation of American Scientists, Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED] So a community’s protection is three documents, each covering a different risk: the ordinance for noise, land, and water; the tariff for the power bill; the benefit agreement for everything negotiated on top. Three paths, and this time they are independent.

### When the name on the building changes

Data centers get sold, and the company that signs is often created just for the one project. The Federation of American Scientists found that transfers often happen without the host government’s consent (Sept. 2026). [VERIFIED] Two lines fix that. One says the obligations run with the land, meaning they attach to the property and bind every later owner. The other requires the county’s written approval before the agreement is handed to someone else. Lancaster’s agreement requires any new owner to take on every obligation (City of Lancaster). [VERIFIED]

### Deals made in the dark

Many of these negotiations start under a nondisclosure agreement, a contract in which officials promise not to discuss the project. A records investigation by public radio’s Gulf States Newsroom found at least 54 of them signed by Louisiana elected officials since early 2024. A university researcher surveying 31 data center projects found nondisclosure agreements in at least 25 (NPR, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

Companies say they need confidentiality for competitive and securities-law reasons, and that concern is real. So is the cost: officials who can’t answer their own voters. One Louisiana parish hosting a $10 billion project used no nondisclosure agreements at all and posted the water, power, and land documents on its website. Lawmakers in Michigan, Oklahoma, Kentucky, and Ohio have introduced bills to ban the practice for data center deals (NPR, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

AnalogySecurity is the difference between a neighbor who says he’ll pay for the fence he backed into and one who leaves the cash with the feed store until the fence is fixed.

Where it breaksThe feed store is down the road and you know the owner. A letter of credit comes from a bank you’ve never dealt with, has an expiration date, and has to be renewed. Somebody at the county has to own that calendar.

## Rung 5. Writing flexibility into the paper

Module 1 showed that the grid is built for its worst hour and has spare room most of the rest of the year. Module 7 showed that a customer able to cut back during those worst hours is easier to connect. A promise to be flexible is valuable. It’s also the easiest promise to make and the hardest to check.

### The flexibility chain, as contract language

Texas shows what the promise looks like when it’s written as a rule. Under Senate Bill 6, customers that connect to the high-voltage grid after December 31, 2025, must be set up so the utility can cut their power during an emergency, when the grid operator is already ordering rotating outages. They must also disclose their backup generators, which the grid operator can direct them to run. A separate program pays large customers of 75 megawatts or more to reduce demand with at least 24 hours’ notice (Texas Legislature, bill analysis, Aug. 2025). [VERIFIED]

Look at what makes those terms enforceable. There’s a size threshold. There’s a named trigger. The switching equipment has to be installed before the customer connects. Nobody has to take the company’s word for it.

A benefit agreement can borrow that shape. Instead of “will be a good grid citizen,” it can say: how many megawatts will be shed, within how many minutes, for how many hours a year, confirmed by the utility’s own meter, with a fixed payment owed for each missed event. [PLAUSIBLE] And it can say how the customer rides through: on batteries, or on diesel generators that the neighbors will hear and breathe. That choice belongs in the paper too.

### Why three

Inside a data center, groups of computers have to agree on what’s true even when one of them fails. A widely used method has each change accepted once a majority of the machines have recorded it, and the group keeps working as long as a majority is still up. The paper that describes it notes that five machines is typical, which lets the group lose two (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014). [VERIFIED]

The smallest group that can lose a member and still have a majority is three: two of three can outvote a failure. Two can’t, because one of two is not a majority.

The same count may apply to whoever watches a deal. If one office holds the reports, and that office is short-staffed or friendly with the company, oversight has a single point of failure. A monitoring committee with three seats that don’t answer to each other, say the county, a resident group, and a paid outside monitor, can lose one and still function. [SPECULATIVE]

AnalogyThree people each keep a copy of the church’s books. If one copy goes missing or gets changed, the other two still agree, and the congregation knows which version to trust.

Where it breaksComputers don’t have friends or grudges. Three people from the same family aren’t three independent copies. Rung 3 applies to committees too.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Do these agreements hold up? Almost none is old enough to have been tested in court. The Federation of American Scientists calls enforcement over time an open problem, and says cleanup obligations at the end of a facility’s life are largely untested. Columbia’s review warns that a small community may not have the money to enforce a contract against a large company, and that some states limit what local governments can sign. Would a pooled legal fund for small counties change that? Would a public registry of signed agreements? Nobody has run the experiment.

## Straight Talk

“Benefit agreements are just PR.”

Partly right. It depends on four clauses.

The skeptics have evidence. Only eight signed data center benefit agreements could be found nationwide in August 2026, and only one was public (Federation of American Scientists). The best-known one asks for “good faith efforts” on local hiring and sets no minimum (Sabin Center, May 2026). [VERIFIED]

But the same agreement caps water at 20,000 gallons a day per campus, holds a $10 million letter of credit, and lets the city seek a court order shutting the site down (City of Lancaster; Sabin Center). [VERIFIED] Those terms aren’t PR. They can be collected.

Ask for it in writing: numbers instead of adjectives, dates on the money, security held by a bank, public reports by a third party, and an enforcement clause the county can use.

## What a good deal is for

The point of all this paper isn’t the paper. The opportunity is not the building. It is the leverage, and what a community does with it.

Rural places are short on particular things: a hospital that can keep its doctors, broadband that reaches the last farm, a training program that lets a young person build a career without leaving. Earlier modules covered each of those. A benefit agreement is where they can be written down. Only 8% of critical access and rural community hospitals use AI-driven predictive analytics (Becker’s, in the Straight Talk library). [VERIFIED] A deal that funds broadband and technology at the local hospital and schools turns a building on the edge of town into something families feel.

October is National Co-op Month. If your power comes from a co-op, the tariff side of this deal is decided by a board you elect. Bring the term sheet to both tables.

County Kit · Module 10

Benefit Agreement Term Sheet

One page to hold a proposed deal against: who signs, what is promised in numbers, when it is paid, what backs it, who checks, and what the county gives in return.

Open the kitOpen the kit
Download PDFDownload PDF

## Ask Earl

AI character

Can my county commissioner sign a nondisclosure agreement about a data center?

“In a lot of places, yes, and plenty have. Whether it’s allowed where you live is a question for your county attorney and your state’s open-records law, not for me. Here’s what I can tell you. A commissioner who can’t talk about a project can’t answer the people who elected him, and that’s where a lot of the anger comes from. They’re right about that part. So ask three things, in writing. Has anyone at the county signed one? What does it cover, and when does it end? And will the full agreement be public, with a hearing, before any vote? If the answer to the last one is no, you’ve learned something about the deal.”

Ready? Five questions.

Get 4 right to pass. Retakes are fine.

Take the self-checkTake the self-check

## Sources

Every source below was opened on Nov. 26, 2026.

- Nolette, V. M. (May 28, 2026), “Community Benefits Agreements and Data Center Development”, Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, Columbia Law School: definition, Lancaster terms, soft language, letter of credit.

- City of Lancaster, Pennsylvania, “About the Community Benefits Agreement”: payment schedule, water cap, reporting, remedies.

- Burns, K. G., & Badea, S. (Aug. 11, 2026), “How We Found Eight Data Center Community Benefit Agreements and Why It Matters”, Federation of American Scientists.

- Federation of American Scientists (Sept. 10, 2026), Before Breaking Ground: A Local Government Guide to Better Data Center Policy and Community Benefits: Festus schedule, Marysville lien, bonds in 4 of 42 actions, cure periods, reporting examples.

- Uptime Institute (April 2021), “Explaining the Uptime Institute’s Tier Classification System”.

- Poles, Chips, and Halls, Volume III, Rung 4: redundancy and the availability rules for parts in series and in parallel.

### Go deeper (rungs 4 and 5), opened Nov. 26, 2026

- Turner Lee, N., & West, D. M. (Jan. 29, 2026), “Why community benefit agreements are necessary for data centers”, Brookings Institution: El Paso abatement, Ohio minimum-demand rule.

- Maryland Association of Counties (Sept. 2, 2026), “Frederick Secures $110M Community Benefits Agreement for Data Center Campus”.

- Miller, N. (Sept. 15, 2026), “Frederick County rejects agreement with data center developer amidst public outcry”, WYPR.

- Frederick County, Maryland, and Quantum Maryland, LLC, draft Development Rights and Responsibilities Agreement (unsigned, 2026), as posted by the Federation of American Scientists.

- Hawkins, D. (Aug. 27, 2026), “NDAs are hiding data center deals, drawing ire from locals, and attention from lawmakers”, NPR and the Gulf States Newsroom.

- Texas Legislature (Aug. 5, 2025), bill analysis, Senate Bill 6 (enrolled).

- Ongaro, D., & Ousterhout, J. (2014), “In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm”, USENIX Annual Technical Conference.

- Straight Talk library, entries 7 and 8 (Columbia Sabin Center, June 2026; Becker’s Hospital Review).

Field Guide · Module 11 of 12 · November 2027

# Small Is Possible

No single town is big enough to matter to the computing industry. Several together can be. Rural America has solved this problem once already, with poles.

The decision it serves: whether to pool computing across a region for public services. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 21 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Pooled demand can pull rural services out of computing’s slow lane.

## Rung 1. The fast lane and the slow lane

For decades, everybody who bought a computer rode the same wave. Each buyer helped pay for the next, faster chip, and the next chip was better at everything. A bank, a farmer, and a video-game company were all pulling the same wagon.

That wagon is splitting. Researchers Neil Thompson and Svenja Spanuth describe computing dividing into a fast lane, where the biggest users get chips designed for their one job, and a slow lane, where everyone else stays on general-purpose chips that improve more slowly (Communications of the ACM, March 2021). [VERIFIED]

The fast lane has a toll. Designing one specialized chip on the newest manufacturing technology cost about $80 million as of 2018, so it only pays for a customer with an enormous amount of the same work to do. The researchers name two kinds of users who end up in the slow lane: those with too little demand to justify the upfront cost, and those whose demand is spread out and hard to coordinate (Thompson & Spanuth, 2021). [VERIFIED]

Read that second description again. Too little demand in any one place, spread thin, hard to coordinate. That’s a rural county’s 911 center, its clinic, its school district, and its courthouse. [PLAUSIBLE]

Rural America has been here before. In the mid-1930s, about nine in ten rural homes had no electric service. Power companies weren’t interested in running lines to a few customers per mile. So farmers formed cooperatives, borrowed through a federal program created in May 1935, and built the lines themselves. By 1953, more than 90% of U.S. farms had electricity (NRECA). [VERIFIED]

Nobody made the farms bigger. They pooled.

AnalogyOne farm can’t justify a grain elevator. Forty farms can. The elevator doesn’t care that each farm is small; it cares what comes down the road in total.

Where it breaksAn elevator built in 1960 may still be standing. Computers are out of date in a handful of years. A group that pools computing has to plan for replacing the equipment from the first day, not the fortieth year.

## Rung 2. Why close matters

Most of what your county does on a computer happens somewhere else. “The cloud” is a plain thing: very large computers in a few big buildings, rented by the hour, reached over the internet. Edge computing is the opposite arrangement: real computing and storage placed near the people and machines that use it (Satyanarayanan, Computer, 2017). [VERIFIED]

The big buildings win on cost, and it’s worth saying so plainly. Putting everything in one place lowers the cost of running each machine (Satyanarayanan, 2017). [VERIFIED] Big sites waste less power, too. Engineers track a number called PUE: the total power a data center draws, divided by the power that reaches its computers. In a 2026 survey the average site reported 1.52, but when sites are weighted by size the figure drops to 1.36, because the largest ones are the most efficient (Uptime Institute, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED]

So why would anyone keep a computer close? The same paper gives four reasons:

- Speed of response. In one study, the average round trip from 260 points around the world to the nearest of Amazon’s big data centers took 74 milliseconds. Some jobs need a reply in a few tens of milliseconds.

- Less to send. A nearby computer can chew through the raw data, such as hours of camera footage, and send on only the result.

- Privacy. Sensitive records can be screened or kept at the first place they land.

- Riding through an outage. A nearby computer can keep a service going when the link to the cloud is down.

(Satyanarayanan, 2017.) [VERIFIED]

For public services, the fourth one carries the most weight. On July 19, 2024, a faulty software update from one security company knocked out computers around the world. Hospitals reported delayed procedures, diverted patients, and cancellations, and some were hit a second way when their local emergency call centers went down (American Hospital Association, July 2024). [VERIFIED]

Be careful with that example. A server down the hall running the same faulty software would have failed the same way. Keeping a machine close doesn’t make it safe. The lesson is narrower: decide ahead of time which services must keep working when the outside world doesn’t, and make sure those few can run without help. [PLAUSIBLE]

AnalogyThe big hospital in the city is efficient because everyone goes through it. The clinic in town is valuable because it is close.

Where it breaksYou can’t move a hospital. You can move a computing job in a blink. So the real answer is both at once: send each job to whichever place does it better.

## Rung 3. Pooling: how small becomes possible

There’s already a name for computing shared by a group of organizations with a common mission. The federal standards agency NIST calls it a community cloud: computing set up for the exclusive use of a specific community of organizations with shared concerns, owned and run by one or more of them, by a hired third party, or by some mix (NIST, Sept. 2011). [VERIFIED] The idea is more than a decade old. It isn’t exotic.

And people already do it:

- Ohio’s schools. State law sets up an education computer network run through regional information technology centers. Each center’s members are school districts and educational service centers, banded together to reach enough students to make the services efficient (Ohio Revised Code 3301.075). The council that coordinates them is itself a 16-member consortium of governments, offering hosting, disaster recovery, and shared services (Management Council of the Ohio Education Computer Network). [VERIFIED]

- Wisconsin’s rural hospitals. The Rural Wisconsin Health Cooperative was incorporated in 1979 and is owned by about forty rural hospitals. Health information technology is one of the services they share (Rural Wisconsin Health Cooperative). [VERIFIED]

- Electric co-ops and broadband. NRECA’s broadband group counted 128 participants in 2025, most of them electric co-ops, serving nearly one million families and businesses across 31 states (NRECA, 2025). [VERIFIED] The co-ops that strung the first wire went back and strung the second.

None of these looks like the data centers in the news. A regional compute co-op would be closer to this: a few racks of ordinary servers in a room the members already own, a handful of shared technicians, and cloud contracts bought together at a better price. [PLAUSIBLE]

What would it run? The kinds of jobs Rung 2 points to: backup copies of county and school records; a fallback for 911 dispatch; the hospital’s and the schools’ day-to-day systems; perhaps a shared AI tool for transcribing and translating that keeps patient and student records inside the region. [SPECULATIVE] Module 6 covered what a rural hospital needs from tools like that.

Field Test: the dishwasher and the sunSome jobs don’t care what time they run. Here’s a way to see why that matters, using only public data. Open the U.S. Energy Information Administration’s Hourly Electric Grid Monitor, pick your region, and look at yesterday. Write down solar’s share of the power being generated at 1 p.m., and again at 8 p.m.: solar divided by the total. Now your dishwasher. A standard ENERGY STAR model may use up to 240 kWh a year over 215 cycles, which is about 1.1 kWh a cycle. [VERIFIED] Multiply that by each share. Same dishes, same energy, different power plants behind it. The regional share is not your house’s exact mix, so your answer is an estimate. [PLAUSIBLE] Computers have jobs like the dishes: backups and record scanning can wait for the right hour. Public data only. Nothing to plug in, nothing to open.

Field Test video. One region, one day of public grid data; figures reported as published. Plug-in meters only.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs make the case that pooling is possible. The next two are about whether it’s wise: what a small site costs, what it’s good for, and how a group of local governments would actually run one. They’re more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them before you bring this idea to a budget meeting.

## Rung 4. The arithmetic of a small site

A small site will never beat a giant one on cost per unit of computing. Rung 2 gave the reasons. So a small site has to earn its keep another way. It pays for presence, not scale.

### What stands in the way

The paper that lists the four advantages of closeness also lists three obstacles: the cost of managing many scattered sites, weaker physical security than a big guarded building, and a chicken-and-egg problem, where nobody builds the sites until the uses exist and nobody builds the uses until the sites exist (Satyanarayanan, 2017). [VERIFIED] The people who say small towns shouldn’t run their own computers are pointing at real problems.

Each one translates directly to a county:

- People. The scarce thing isn’t the machine. It’s the technician who knows how to keep it patched, backed up, and secure. One county can’t afford three of them. Six member organizations might. [PLAUSIBLE] This is the main thing pooling buys.

- Security. A server in a courthouse closet is easier to walk up to than one behind a fence and a guard. A shared site can afford a locked room, cameras, and a log of who went in.

- Who goes first. Somebody has to be the anchor: usually the member with the most at stake, such as the hospital or the largest school district.

### A test for what stays close

Run each service through the four advantages from Rung 2. Does it need an answer in a split second? Does it produce far more raw data than anyone needs to send? Is the data sensitive enough that it shouldn’t leave? Must it keep working when the outside link is down? A service that answers yes to none of them belongs in the cloud, where it’s cheaper. A service that answers yes to one or more is a candidate to keep close.

Most groups will end up with both. NIST has a name for that too: a hybrid cloud, two or more separate clouds tied together so that data and programs can move between them (NIST, Sept. 2011). [VERIFIED]

### Three sites, not one

Module 10 showed that copies aren’t independence. The same holds here. One server room is a single point of failure, however carefully it’s built. Two rooms in two towns on two different power lines, plus a copy in the cloud, makes three places that are unlikely to fail together. [PLAUSIBLE] Pooling is what makes the second room affordable.

### Small can be flexible

The Field Test showed that the same job can lean on different power plants depending on the hour. A small site can use that. Backups, scanning old records, and updating software don’t need to happen at five in the afternoon in July. Scheduling them for hours when the grid has room is the flexibility chain from Module 7 at small scale, and it costs nothing but planning. [PLAUSIBLE]

AnalogyA town doesn’t keep a fire truck because it’s the cheapest way to put out fires per fire. It keeps one because the truck in the city is forty minutes away.

Where it breaksA fire truck is supposed to sit idle. A server that sits idle is wasted money. So a small site should be kept busy with work that can wait, and cleared the moment something urgent comes in.

## Rung 5. Who owns it, and who votes

The hard part of a compute co-op isn’t the computers. It’s the bylaws.

### Borrow the co-op rulebook

Cooperatives run on seven published principles. Three of them do most of the work here (NRECA). [VERIFIED]

- Democratic member control. Members control the organization, and in a local co-op each member gets one vote.

- Members’ economic participation. Members put in the capital fairly, and any surplus goes to reserves, to growth, or back to members in proportion to their use.

- Cooperation among cooperatives. Co-ops get stronger by working through shared regional and national structures.

Ohio’s school network adds a fourth idea worth copying. State law says no rule may stop a district from buying computer services from any other public or private vendor (Ohio Revised Code 3301.075). [VERIFIED] Members stay because the service is worth it, not because they’re locked in.

### The decisions to write down

- Who can join? County, cities, school districts, the hospital, the library, the electric co-op.

- One member, one vote, or votes by use? A hospital that uses half the capacity and a library that uses 2% won’t see this the same way.

- Whose data is it? Each member should own its data outright and be able to take it and leave.

- Who pays to replace the machines? Equipment runs on the chip clock. A reserve funded every year, from the first year, is the difference between a co-op and a one-time grant that rusts. [PLAUSIBLE]

- What legal form? A cooperative, or a council of governments like Ohio’s. That one is a question for the members’ attorneys.

### A two-question screen

Here’s a rough way to decide which services to look at first. Ask how badly the service is stuck in the slow lane: is anyone ever going to build a product for a buyer this small? Then ask how thin the demand is: how few users per square mile? A service that scores high on both, such as dispatch for a large, empty county, is where pooling has the most to offer and where the market is least likely to show up without it. [SPECULATIVE] It’s a way to sort a list, not a finding.

And one link back to Module 10. A community negotiating a benefit agreement with a large data center could ask for the seed of something like this: a room, a fiber connection, and a few years of funding for shared public computing. [SPECULATIVE] We know of no agreement that has done it yet.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] How many members, or how many people served, does a compute co-op need before it covers its costs? Can a rural region hire and keep the technicians? Does keeping an AI tool inside the region measurably improve privacy or uptime, or does it only feel safer? Who insures it? These don’t have answers yet. They’re good questions for a state university, an extension office, or the first region willing to try and publish what happens.

## Straight Talk

“Small towns can’t run their own compute.”

Partly right. Alone, usually. Together, some already do.

The objection has weight. Big sites are more efficient: an average PUE of 1.52 falls to 1.36 when sites are weighted by size (Uptime Institute, Aug. 2026). And the research that makes the case for computing close to home also lists what stands in the way: management cost, security, and nobody wanting to go first (Satyanarayanan, 2017). [VERIFIED]

But pooled public computing isn’t hypothetical. Ohio law organizes school districts into regional technology centers, and about forty rural Wisconsin hospitals have owned a cooperative that shares technology services since 1979 (Ohio Revised Code 3301.075; Rural Wisconsin Health Cooperative). [VERIFIED]

Ask for it in writing: before anyone buys hardware, a list of the services that must keep running when the outside link is down, and the names of the neighbors willing to share the cost.

## What this does at your kitchen table

Nobody outside a county office will ever see a server room. What families see is whether the 911 call gets answered on a bad night, whether the clinic can pull up a chart when the internet is down, and whether the school’s systems are running on Monday morning.

There’s a job in it, too. Module 8 was blunt that large data centers bring few permanent jobs. A shared regional site brings fewer still, perhaps a handful. But they’re skilled jobs that have to be done locally, by people who answer to local boards. [PLAUSIBLE]

November is budget season. If the idea is worth an hour of your board’s time, the concept sheet below is the one page to bring.

One page to test the idea before anyone spends money: who the members would be, which services belong close to home, what gets pooled, who votes, and who pays to replace the equipment.

## Ask Earl

AI character

Could our county run its own computers instead of renting everything from the cloud?

“By itself? Probably not well, and I’d be wary of anybody who tells you it’s easy. The folks who say small towns can’t do this are right about the hard part: it isn’t the machines, it’s keeping good people to run them. But that’s the same thing they said about stringing wire to farms. One farm couldn’t do it. A few hundred farms with a board and a loan could. So don’t ask whether your county can. Ask which neighbors would go in with you, the hospital, the schools, the co-op, and which two or three services you can’t afford to lose when the outside link goes down. Start there, and keep renting the rest. Whether it pencils out for your county is a question for your own budget people, not for me.”

## Sources

Every source below was opened on Nov. 26, 2026.

- Thompson, N. C., & Spanuth, S. (March 2021), “The Decline of Computers as a General Purpose Technology”, Communications of the ACM, 64(3): fast lane and slow lane, the $80 million chip, who ends up in the slow lane.

- NRECA, “History”: nine in ten rural homes without service in the mid-1930s; the 1935 federal program; more than 90% of farms electrified by 1953.

- Satyanarayanan, M. (2017), “The Emergence of Edge Computing”, Computer, 50(1): definition, the four advantages, the three obstacles, the 74-millisecond measurement.

- Ohio Revised Code, section 3301.075 (effective Oct. 3, 2023), and Management Council of the Ohio Education Computer Network.

- Rural Wisconsin Health Cooperative, “RWHC Overview”. The page gives the member count as both forty and forty-one; we say “about forty.”

- NRECA Broadband, 2025 Broadband Annual Report: 128 participants, nearly one million families and businesses, 31 states.

- U.S. Energy Information Administration, “About the EIA-930 data” (Hourly Electric Grid Monitor), and ENERGY STAR, “Dishwashers Key Product Criteria” (effective July 19, 2023): 240 kWh a year, 215 cycles.

Field Guide · Module 12 of 12 · December 2027

# The Three Clocks

Eleven modules, one picture. Three clocks run at three speeds, and only one of them is yours to set.

The decision it serves: writing a 12-month local plan. About 15 minutes to read, plus 10 for the Go deeper rungs.

Listen to this module
Narration: AI voice

The whole module, rungs 1 to 5, read aloud. About 18 minutes. Read the script · Download MP3

Carry this

Compute grows at chip speed, power at grid speed; the gap is where you bargain.

## Rung 1. Three clocks, three speeds

Everything in this Field Guide fits on three clocks.

The first is the chip clock. Demand for computing moves fast. U.S. data centers used about 4.4% of the country’s electricity in 2023. Their load had roughly tripled over the decade before, and a national laboratory projects it will double or triple again by 2028, to somewhere between 6.7% and 12% (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Dec. 2024). [VERIFIED] Five years, from one size to two or three times that size. That is chip speed.

The second is the grid clock. Power plants, substations, and lines move slow. A new power project now waits more than five years between asking to connect and switching on, in the regions that report data. At the end of 2025, about 2,061 gigawatts of projects were standing in that line (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, July 2026). [VERIFIED] Big new customers face studies and upgrades of their own (Module 1, Rung 5).

The third clock is yours. It’s the county’s calendar: the planning commission’s meeting dates, the budget hearing, the co-op’s annual meeting, the next election. Nothing gets built in your county until something on that calendar says yes.

A company on the chip clock is in a hurry. The grid it needs is not. And the permission it needs sits on a calendar that you and your neighbors control.

AnalogyThe seed company has a new variety every spring. An orchard takes years to bear. And what goes in the ground on your place this year is your decision, made on your schedule.

Where it breaksA farmer who waits a season loses one season. A county that waits can lose its turn: the project goes elsewhere, or the decision moves to the state. The third clock is yours only if you’re ready when it strikes.

## Rung 2. The gap is where you bargain

Put the first two clocks side by side. One side wants power in two years. The other can deliver it in five or more. The distance between them is the gap.

That gap is where the money is, because whoever can close it fastest wins the business. It’s where the conflict is, because closing it fast tempts people to skip steps. And it’s where your room to bargain is, because a developer who needs speed has reasons to accept terms. [PLAUSIBLE]

Three habits follow from that.

- Treat hurry as information. “We need a vote this month” tells you the other side’s clock is running. In Frederick County, Maryland, residents got ten days to comment on a proposal worth more than $110 million; the county executive rejected it (WYPR, Sept. 2026; Module 10). [VERIFIED] A good deal survives thirty more days of reading.

- Plan in ranges. The 2028 forecast above spans nearly a factor of two. Nobody knows which end is right. A plan that only works at one end is no plan at all.

- Write your terms before the phone rings. A county that already has its ordinance, its questions, and its priorities on paper negotiates on its own clock. A county that starts writing after the application arrives negotiates on the developer’s.

## Rung 3. Three chains, three asks

Underneath the year’s twelve topics are three chains of cause and effect. Each one turns into something a community can ask for in writing.

### The heat chain

Every watt a chip uses becomes heat, and moving that heat outdoors takes more power and sometimes water (Modules 3 and 4). The average data center draws about 1.52 watts for every watt that reaches its computers; weighted by size, the figure is 1.36 (Uptime Institute, Aug. 2026). [VERIFIED] So a watt saved at the chip saves the cooling behind it and the generation behind that.

The ask: efficiency and cooling, in the ordinance. Name the measure and where it’s taken, require it reported every year, and require the cooling design to be stated, because the design decides the water.

### The capital chain

A very large customer needs a substation and lines that are paid off over decades. If that customer shrinks or leaves, the unpaid cost can land on everyone else (Module 2). As of May 2026, 23 states had approved at least one large-load tariff to prevent that (Columbia Sabin Center, in the Straight Talk library). [VERIFIED]

The ask: a large-load tariff with a minimum bill, collateral posted up front, an exit fee, and a contract as long as the debt.

### The flexibility chain

The grid is built for its worst hour and has room in most of the others (Module 1). A customer that can cut back in the worst hours is easier and cheaper to connect (Module 7).

The ask: flexibility as a condition of connecting. Curtailment hours in the contract, batteries before more diesel engines, and limits on generator hours in the permit.

Three chains, three documents: the ordinance, the tariff, and the agreement. Module 10 explained why you want all three, each standing by itself.

Field Test: the year’s logThis month’s test is to look back at the other eleven. If you ran them, lay your readings side by side: the volts your outlet lost when the microwave started, the dishwasher cycle at two prices, the laptop’s watts idle and busy, the dew point on the porch, the condenser’s sound at four distances, the words a laptop wrote per joule, the window unit’s watts through the peak hour, the dead battery you found by halving, the delay at the far fence, the mesh point at the modem, and the dishwasher against the sun. For each one, write three things: what you measured, with what, and whether it matched what the module said. Where it didn’t match, that’s the interesting line. Phone-app readings are estimates. [PLAUSIBLE] One house is never a national figure. Plug-in and handheld meters only. Never open equipment.

Field Test video. A year of readings from one household, reported as measured, including the ones that didn’t match. Plug-in meters only.

## Go deeper

The first three rungs are the year in review. The next two turn it into a plan: what a county does in each quarter, and how to plan honestly when the forecasts disagree. They’re more technical, but every term is defined. Skip them and you can still pass the self-check; read them if you’re the one who has to write the plan.

## Rung 4. A twelve-month plan, quarter by quarter

A county plan for this isn’t a study. It’s a short list of facts to gather, rules to write, and dates to hit, with a name next to each. Here is one way to lay it out. The order matters more than the months. [PLAUSIBLE]

### First quarter: know where you stand

- Fill in the Know Your Utility sheet (Module 1): who owns the wires, when the board is elected, and your system’s peak demand.

- Ask the utility, in writing, how many large-load requests are pending and how big the largest is as a share of that peak.

- Ask whether anyone in county government has signed a nondisclosure agreement (Module 10).

- Mark the year’s fixed dates: budget adoption, planning commission meetings, the co-op annual meeting, filing deadlines for board seats.

### Second quarter: write the rules

- Water: a disclosure requirement covering cooling type, peak and average gallons, source, and a drought clause (Module 4).

- Noise and land: a decibel limit at the property line, setbacks, generator test hours, and third-party monitoring (Module 5).

- Efficiency: the yearly reporting from the heat chain above.

Spring is planning and zoning season in most places. An ordinance written before any application is on file is ordinary lawmaking. One written after can look like it was aimed at a single company, and may be challenged that way. [PLAUSIBLE]

### Third quarter: set the terms

- The tariff: if your utility has no large-load tariff, ask the co-op board or the state commission for one, using the Module 2 checklist.

- Flexibility: the curtailment and battery terms from Module 7.

- Jobs: local-hire targets, apprenticeships, and a community college partner (Module 8).

### Fourth quarter: decide what you want

- Fill in the benefit agreement term sheet with your own priorities before anyone offers theirs (Module 10).

- Name the three things your community is shortest on. For many rural places that’s the hospital, broadband, and a way for young people to train and stay (Modules 6, 8, and 9).

- Ask the neighbors whether any public computing is worth pooling (Module 11).

- Set next year’s dates, and publish the plan.

### Triggers

Most counties will never get the call. So the plan should say what moves the county from watching to acting. Three reasonable triggers: a pending request above a set share of the utility’s peak; a rezoning or annexation inquiry for a large tract; a request that any official sign a nondisclosure agreement. [SPECULATIVE] When one trips, the plan’s owner calls a public meeting. That’s all a trigger has to do.

AnalogyA county emergency plan doesn’t predict the tornado. It says who opens the shelter, who has the keys, and what siren means go.

Where it breaksA tornado isn’t negotiating with you. A developer is, and will read your plan. That’s fine. A published plan tells serious developers what a yes looks like and saves both sides time.

## Rung 5. Planning when nobody knows

The numbers in Rung 1 came with a warning: the 2028 range runs from 6.7% to 12%. People who study this for a living disagree by nearly a factor of two about a date that is close. Past that date, they disagree by more.

### Why the forecasts are wide

History gives reasons to doubt both extremes. From 2010 to 2018, the world’s data centers did about 6.5 times as much computing while their electricity use rose only about 6%, because efficiency improved almost as fast as demand (Masanet et al., 2020, in the Straight Talk library). [VERIFIED] AI broke that balance after 2017. Whether efficiency catches up again, nobody can say. [SPECULATIVE]

The grid clock has the same uncertainty. The line of projects waiting to connect shrank by 10% in 2025, with more than 750 gigawatts withdrawn. Of everything that asked to connect from 2000 to 2020, about 13% had been built by the end of 2025 and 75% had dropped out (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, July 2026). [VERIFIED] Most of what is announced never arrives.

### What a plan can do about that

Ask for three cases, not one. Any forecast your utility or a developer shows you should come as a low, a base, and a high. Then test each term in your plan against all three.

- If the boom keeps going, the risk is strain: on rates, water, land, and the grid. The heat and flexibility asks protect you.

- If the boom ends, the risk is being left with the bill: a substation built for a customer who never came, or left early. The capital ask protects you. A minimum bill, collateral, and an exit fee matter most in exactly the future where the optimists were wrong. [PLAUSIBLE]

- Either way, an enforcement clause is worth the same. Module 10’s test doesn’t depend on the forecast.

That’s the reason to write terms that hold in every case, and not to bet the county on one.

### Where the critics were right this year

This guide has tried to say so each time. Permanent jobs are few (Module 8). Tax breaks can erase much of the promised revenue (Module 10). Noise complaints are real, and so is local water strain from some cooling designs (Modules 4 and 5). Deals are often made in secret (Module 10). Rate risk is real where power is tight (Module 2). None of that is settled by enthusiasm. All of it can be addressed in writing, and that has been the argument of the whole year.

Still open [SPECULATIVE] Will the three clocks stay this far apart? Faster grid studies, on-site power, or a slowdown in AI spending could each narrow the gap, and with it the leverage. Will states leave these decisions with counties, or take them? Does a published county plan attract better proposals, or just fewer? We don’t know. If your county writes one, tell us what happened, and we’ll publish it with the grade it earns.

## Straight Talk

“The AI boom will be over soon.”

It depends, and your plan shouldn’t.

It might be. Forecasts for 2028 differ by nearly a factor of two, from 6.7% to 12% of U.S. electricity (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Dec. 2024), and most projects that ask to connect to the grid are never built: 75% of the capacity requested from 2000 to 2020 was withdrawn (Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, July 2026). [VERIFIED]

But “it’ll blow over” isn’t a plan either. If the boom ends, the communities hurt most will be the ones that built for a customer and didn’t secure the bill. [PLAUSIBLE]

Ask for it in writing: low, base, and high cases in any forecast, and terms that protect you in all three.

## What the year was for

Infrastructure is a means. The end is a hospital that stays open, a farm that stays profitable, and a kid who can build a career without leaving home.

None of that comes from a building at the edge of town. It comes from what a community asks for and gets in writing: broadband that stays, a training program with a real employer at the end of it, technology money for the clinic and the schools, a co-op whose members aren’t paying for someone else’s substation. The opportunity is not the building. It is the leverage.

If you’ve passed all twelve self-checks, the Field Certificate is yours, with your county’s name on it. Take it to your board along with the one-page plan below.

County Kit · Module 12

County AI Infrastructure Plan

One page for the year ahead: where you stand, the three clocks in your county, which rules are written and which aren’t, what you want from any deal, and who does what each quarter.

Open the kitOpen the kit
Download PDFDownload PDF

## Ask Earl

AI character

This is a lot. Where do I start?

“Same place a lineman starts: find out what you’re standing under before you touch anything. Three phone calls. Call your co-op or utility and ask what its peak is and whether any big customers have asked to hook up. Call the county and ask when the planning board meets and whether anybody’s signed a confidentiality paper. Then call one neighbor who’ll go to the meeting with you. That’s the first quarter of the plan, and it costs you an afternoon. I won’t tell you whether any project is good for your county. That’s yours to decide. But decide it on your own calendar, and ask for it in writing.”

Ready? Five questions.

## Sources

Every source below was opened on Nov. 26, 2026, except Straight Talk library entries, which are cited as the library.

- Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Dec. 20, 2024; posted Jan. 15, 2025), “Berkeley Lab Report Evaluates Increase in Electricity Demand from Data Centers”, on Shehabi et al. (2024): 4.4% in 2023; 6.7% to 12% by 2028; load roughly tripled over the past decade.

- Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (July 1, 2026), “Backlog of power plants seeking transmission grid connection eased somewhat in 2025 amidst high withdrawals”, on Queued Up: 2026 Edition: 2,061 GW; more than five years to operation; 10% decline; more than 750 GW withdrawn; 13% built and 75% withdrawn.

- Uptime Institute (Aug. 6, 2026), “The growing PUE advantage of larger data centers” (UII Update 518).

- Miller, N. (Sept. 15, 2026), “Frederick County rejects agreement with data center developer amidst public outcry”, WYPR.

- Straight Talk library, entries 6, 7, and 9 (Shehabi et al., 2024; Columbia Sabin Center, June 2026; Masanet et al., 2020).

- Poles, Chips, and Halls, Version 1.1, Part IV, for the three clocks and the heat, capital, and flexibility chains, as summarized in the Grid & Grain playbook.

### Go deeper (rungs 4 and 5)

- The quarter-by-quarter plan draws on the County Kits from Modules 1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, and 11. It is a suggested order, graded PLAUSIBLE, not a legal requirement.
